Fresh Yorkers woke up this Thanksgiving morning to drizzly, gray skies along with winds that had sidewalks covered in dead, yellow leaves, though the weather throughout the pre-noon hours was hardly the fearsome nor’easter blast that prompted the postponement till Saturday of Macy’s 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade.

Still, with wind levels of up to 23 mph – and gusts considerably stronger – the postponement appears to have been justified, and the worst of the storm is yet to come.

The impact of the postponement on performances that had been scheduled for today – marching bands, celebrity appearances, the significant Broadway medley involving nine different highlights – was still be dealt with as of this morning. Will Coss, Macy’s executive producer of the parade, told the Today show this morning that organizers are “actively working through all the pieces of our parade, but I have to say there’s an overwhelming positive response.” Related Stories News Mayor Zohran Mamdani Notes Famed Balloons Will Soar Again At Rescheduled Macy's Parade: "It's The Only Inflation We Support In Newly introduced York City" News Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade Postponed To Saturday Due To Severe Weather; NBC Will Rerun 2025 Parade On Thursday.

Coss continued, “Our performers, our talent, our performance groups, our bands, we’re all coming together to try to figure this out, and we’re optimistic that we’re going to have a really successful parade on Saturday morning.” Watch on Deadline.

Recent findings suggest that while Coss didn’t specify which performances are on schedule, Deadline can confirm that the Broadway medley that was planned in lieu of the traditional individual show performances is a go for Saturday. What Macy’s is calling the “All-Star Broadway Thanksgiving Day Celebration” will go on as planned, with performers from The Lost Boys, The Rocky Horror Show, Wicked, Schmigadoon!, Aladdin, The Book of Mormon and Chicago confirmed. (Hamiilton and the 30th-anniversary tribute to Rent have not weighed in yet, but sources say they are expected to participate).

Paddington the Musical is confirmed to participate in the Saturday broadcast as a separate float, as originally intended.

On Instagram today, Sherri Shepherd, presently portraying Genie in Broadway’s Aladdin, wrote, “Winds won’t stop our participation in the Macys 100 Thanksgiving Day Parade, so tune in Saturday at 8:30am on NBC to catch myself and the cast of Aladdin perform!!”.

On the Schmigadoon! IG page, Brad Oscar, dressed and in character as the Mayor, stated in a video, “As mayor of Schmigadoon, I have a proclamation: The Macy’s 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade will be postponed until Saturday at 8:30 a.m. on NBC. See you there.”.

The Book of Mormon had a simple message on its IG page about the date switch: “Ready and psyched.”.

Industry observers note that as for other non-Broadway performers originally scheduled for Thursday, reports are filtering in piecemeal on whether they’ll make the move to Saturday. The Fresh York Post has reported that Smash Mouth will perform, and Holly Robinson Peete and Rodney Peete are expected as well, as are the Radio City Rockettes. Other announcements should be coming in over the next day or two.

As for the marching bands, again, piecemeal reports. Texas’ Pride of Pearland Marching Band reportedly raised an extra $350,000 in community donations to cover the additional housing and transportation costs to stay until Saturday, while other marching bands were either still scrambling or had made the decision to bow out of the event due to logistics. In the latter group are the Campo Verde High School Marching Band and some members of the Bowling Green State University Marching Band that were participating in a all-star band group.

Sony's line of soundbars can cost a lot of money — but it's the mid-range and cheap offerings that we recommend the most. This, the Theater Bar 7, is the mid-range bar, and it offers some great value for money.

For one, the 5.1.2 Dolby Atmos sound is very good. The included sub offers some extra low-end for those all-important explosions in action movies, and the surround sound is immersive and well produced. The dialogue department is where the soundbar really shines. Speech is clear and easily discernible over whatever else is going on on-screen.

In a recent development, there are also some useful smart features built in. You can connect to your Wi-Fi to stream music to the bar, and adjust settings from the app on your phone. As long as you don't expect the best musical sound, of course — as with so many soundbars, this is not a musical powerhouse but a rectangular movie hero. And that's OK.

Those with bigger TVs might also struggle slightly with the size. It's quite a compact soundbar, and that can affect the perception of sound in space when the image above it is much larger. Thankfully, the solid surround sound does a good job of keeping the effect to a minimum.

It should be noted that the Theater Bar 7 is not a cheap soundbar, but it's a great way of getting immersive sound without spending thousands on one of the range-topping devices.

Recent findings suggest that setupFor any normal movie or TV watching, setting up the bar is very easy. Plug it into the power, and then into the HDMI ARC port on your TV. Plug in the subwoofer and everything connects together with no hassle at all.

Nor is connecting the bar to the internet. Download the app, and then follow the on-screen instructions to get everything working properly. We recommend you dip into the settings menu from there and turn the bass up, and raise the surround height to 10. That gave us the best sound, although your room might require some fine tweaking.

How massive is itThis is a fairly compact soundbar, measuring 37.5 inches long. That means that it's going to be dwarfed by larger TVs, but those measuring around 55 inches or smaller are going to be fine. Our testing TV is 55 inches, for example, and everything was fine.

According to recent reports, the subwoofer is thin and compact too, so you don't need as much space as you might for some of the competition. It fits perfectly beside a TV unit without sticking out like a sore thumb.

In a recent development, are there any extrasThere's one very major extra in the box beside the remote control — that lovely big subwoofer for the low stuff. There aren't any extra surround speakers though, because they're all built into the bar itself.

Recent findings suggest that features-wise, though, you've got the mobile app to go with Bluetooth and wired audio connections. You can stream music to the bar from around the house, should you want some music when you're not watching movies. You can also use the app to change key settings of the bar, like sound profiles and bass levels.

SoundSony's audio chops are well documented, and the Theater Bar 7 just continues the legacy. There's some lovely bass on offer here, with impact and depth whenever the action on screen gets thick and fast. We used the app to dial in the bass a bit, though; out of the box it was tuned a bit low. Your mileage may vary, of course.

It has been revealed that the dialogue was what really impressed here, though. Speech was clear and bright no matter what was going on around it, be that a fighter plane screeching through the skies or a car chase in the Batmobile. That's not to say it's ever in your face. When the goings get calmer, the voices adjust to match. You'll never miss a word.

Sources indicate that not everything is rosy, as it generally isn't with most soundbars. Music playback is disappointing, with merely an "OK" in our review. It's not bad, but there's no drive to the music as you'll find with movies and TV shows. A shame, but not unexpected.

According to recent reports, if you want a true surround sound package in one unit, then the 1300XMK2 could be just what you've been looking for. Its extra speakers attach to the bar itself, and then you can move them into position when you want to watch a movie. It's not cheap, but it's a movie monster.

There’s not really such a thing as a “bargain” when it comes to home surround sound. Instead, there’s value — and the JBL Bar 1300XMK2 brings the value unlike just about anything. Flexibility, a more affordable price than the key competition, and, of course, great sound.

The two ends of the soundbar can be disconnected and placed around the room, powered by their own internal batteries. If you don’t have the space for a traditional setup, this is a great way to enjoy immersive Dolby Atmos sound without a more permanent (and expensive) solution.

The soundbar itself is quite large, however. It’s very deep and rather long with its surrounds attached, so you’ll need a long TV stand and massive TV to make sure it doesn’t look out of place. There’s a subwoofer in the box that you’ll need to find space for as well.

The sound is great. It’s immersive, directional, deep and clear. We loved it when watching a wide range of movies, from action to romance. There’s little this soundbar can’t do.

Sources indicate that setupFirst off, hit the gym before you place this soundbar anywhere. This is a 26-pound behemoth, so you might even want two people to lift it into place on your TV stand. There are some extra setup quirks as well, but they’re easily mitigated thanks to the good instructions and user-friendly design.

Once you’ve plugged the soundbar and subwoofer into the wall, you’ll hook the soundbar into the eARC port of your TV. The soundbar and sub should find each other automatically, but if not, use the connection button on the sub.

Industry observers note that if you want to use the surrounds, pull them off the soundbar and place them around your room. Sound adjustment is done automatically. If you have any wireless connection issues, re-attach them to the soundbar to reset everything.

Streaming and Wi-Fi are handled by JBL’s ONE app. It’s super easy; we had no problems at all getting everything connected and working.

Industry observers note that how big is itThere’s no two ways around it — the 1300XMK2 is a very big soundbar. At 40 inches, the soundbar is wide, and that's without taking extra surrounds into account. It’s very deep too, so you’ll want to make sure that there’s enough space on your TV stand that way. If not, we’d recommend wall mounting the TV.

In a recent development, this is a bar suited to much larger TVs, 65-inch at a minimum. Otherwise you’ll risk the bar looking too big, and your TV small.

Industry observers note that thankfully, you won’t have to worry about how tall the bar is. It’s short enough that most TVs will amply clear the top, so you don’t have to worry about the soundbar blocking the view. Just bear in mind that you’ll also want space for the surround speakers behind your seating position — they’re not going to work if they’re in front of you.

Are there any extrasYou get everything you need in the box. There’s the bar itself, along with the surround speakers. Unlike other models, from the likes of Sonos, this is a major bonus and means you don’t have to buy any further devices for some lovely Dolby Atmos sound.

It has been revealed that there’s also a subwoofer in the box, along with all the cables you’d ever need for just about any circumstance. There’s a controller in the box, although we found that the JBL ONE app was a perfectly serviceable way of controlling the sound — or your TV remote through the eARC port.

SoundWith 23 drivers powering 11.1.4 channels, you’d hope the 1300XMK2 sounded good. And, sure enough, the bar sounds excellent. Those extra surrounds make sure that the sound is immersive and massive, while the sub adds impressive depth and bass.

The planes flying in Top Gun: Maverick made the room shake, and the soundtrack was bombastic during testing. The whole movie placed our tester directly in the movie.

Object placement is good too, making sure that everything is kept in the right place.

The soundbar was pretty good for music too, making soundtracks sound great, although it struggled slightly more with stereo tracks — but it's still better than most soundbars.

It has been revealed that want everything in one box but don't want to spend every single dollar you have? The QS750F is a great option, with extra surround speakers and a subwoofer for less than $1000.

Soundbars are expensive — there’s no way around that. You want to achieve the best bang-for-buck sound, right? Enter the Samsung QS750F. For a relatively low MSRP of $899, the QS750F gives you a soundbar, two rears, and a subwoofer, which is considerably more generous than Sonos or JBL.

As a result, the QS750F blows the competition out of the park. For under $1k, you get cinematic sound, with enviable width and immense bass. The QS750F sounds so good that we forgot we were supposed to be reviewing it.

Although it’s just a 5.1.2 channel configuration — considerably fewer speakers than JBL’s monstrous 1300XMK2, which boasts 11.1.4 channels and costs almost double — you probably wouldn’t be able to notice the difference.

SetupAs with every other soundbar, setup is a relatively quick process. Once the soundbar, subwoofer, and rears are unpackaged, simply connect everything to power and plug the soundbar into your TV using HDMI eARC.

Recent findings suggest that unlike JBL’s collection of premium soundbars, the QS750F’s rears aren’t truly “wireless” — sure, they connect to the soundbar wirelessly, but the left speaker must be connected to power. This is only an concern if you’re short on power outlets, extension cables, or if you want a particularly cable-free setup. Even so, you’re not going to get a better multi-speaker setup for less, so we think this is a worthy sacrifice.

The subwoofer is wireless, so don’t worry about needing to connect that to the soundbar with a wire. It’ll automatically connect.

Sources indicate that how significant is itAs you might expect, the QS750F is a large soundbar. This is true of pretty much every high-power soundbar — they’re designed to be able to fill large rooms with both size and physical presence.

The soundbar is 46 inches long and ten inches deep, so you’ll need to ensure it fits on your TV stand/wall mount and that your TV is major enough. I’d recommend anything from 55 inches up.

Industry observers note that the subwoofer is effectively a 10 x 10 x 10-inch cube. We’d recommend positioning the subwoofer around 12 inches from the walls on all sides. You’ll need to play around with spacing to figure out the optimal position. Some setups come with configuration modes in the relevant app, but Samsung locks its proprietary Space Fit Pro behind post-2021 AI-powered Samsung TVs.

Are there any extrasThe QS750F comes with everything you need for a Dolby Atmos all-in-one setup. You get the soundbar, subwoofer, and two rears.

It has been revealed that you also get AirPlay, Google Cast, and smart home features in the SmartThings app, which we’d recommend downloading. You can easily adjust playback modes and listening styles — movie, music, gaming, voice enhancement — to find what pleases you.

SoundAlright, now onto the most vital part of any soundbar: its audio output. Thankfully, you’ll be pleased to know that the QS750F sounds utterly fantastic.

As the QS750F is a large soundbar, it’s intended for use in a large room. The side-firing speakers in the soundbar itself and the powerful subwoofer work together to create a wide soundscape worthy of a movie theater. Although there’s not as much height as width, the soundbar’s Dolby Atmos performance is still admirable.

According to recent reports, the dialogue performance is a clear standout, though: I was never left wondering what was being mentioned thanks to voice enhancement mode. This feature isolated dialogue well, and ensured even the moodiest and broodiest speech was crystal clear.

Industry observers note that most audiophiles will be the first to admit that soundbars aren’t ideal for playing music — me included — but the QS750F didn’t balk at the challenge. Although I’d much rather listen to music via my bookshelf speakers or headphones, the QS750F played every song with rich, pulsing bass, and would be good enough for a quick listening session or party.

Sonos' compact soundbar brings excellent sound with a slightly higher price tag than the old model — but the app is still a bit tetchy. Still, this great-sounding bar is a great option for Sonos homes with living rooms too small for the Arc Ultra.

The Sonos Beam Ultra feels like a statement of intent. The app works better than ever, the sound is incredible, and the surround sound straight out of the bar itself is top-notch. There are still problems — music sounds bad, and a lack of HDMI passthrough is a shame.

Recent findings suggest that but this is Sonos on top form. The design is great, bringing that Sonos minimalism to a smaller bar than the enormous Arc Ultra. It’s perhaps a little more plain than some of the brand's other devices, but it's a handsome thing that’ll blend in perfectly with any living room decor. The traditional black and white colorways are still the only options, unfortunately.

Recent findings suggest that and then there’s the way it sounds. It increases the Dolby Atmos effect with height channels, making for a more immersive movie experience that lands you directly in the center of the action. Add in a few extra Sonos speakers for a full surround setup and you have the perfect movie-watching experience for a smaller space.

It is expensive, mind you. The Beam was never cheap, but this one ups the price ante to make it a less compelling buy than other bars around this size class. And while Sonos app is much better than it was in early 2025, I’ve had more problems with it than our tester, with dropouts and other problems.

Industry observers note that setup is super easy. You just plug the soundbar into a wall outlet, and then an HDMI cable into the eARC port on the back of your TV. That could be it, if you’re not interested in any of the extra Sonos features.

Recent findings suggest that to finish setup you’ll need to use the Sonos app, which is now much improved. From there you can do sound tuning setup amongst other things, like connecting extra Sonos surround speakers or a subwoofer for extra bass. It’s simple and easy to do, and the app will take you through it step by step.

Recent findings suggest that this is also where you’ll stream audio to the device or adjust any settings. There’s no remote that comes with the soundbar — everything goes through the Sonos app.

The Beam Ultra really stretches the “compact” soundbar thing. It measures around 30 inches wide, making it a larger soundbar than some of the smaller compact options. That makes it perfect for TVs around 55 inches and smaller, though Sonos says it works for TVs up to 65 inches.

For larger spaces and TVs you’ll want the larger Sonos Arc Ultra.

In a recent development, in the box, you’ll find the soundbar, a power cable, and the HDMI cable. That’s it. There’s no remote, no wall mount — just the soundbar.

Industry observers note that you can buy extras. Sonos speakers, the Era 100, 300, Sub Mini and Sub 4 all work as surround options for the Beam Ultra. I’d recommend the Era 100 and Sub Mini for smaller rooms if you want to increase the surround capability of the bar.

Unfortunately, everything has to come from Sonos’ rather enclosed ecosystem. You cannot add a separate 3rd-party subwoofer, for example. Shame.

The Beam Ultra is the best Dolby Atmos soundbar for its size. There’s real height to the sound here, making for a far better immersive bubble than other similarly sized bars. There’s width too — it’s a great way to watch your favorite movies.

Unfortunately, stereo music sounds straight up bad. That’s a shame, given that Sonos nailed it with the Arc Ultra — if you want to listen to music, you’re better off grabbing a stereo pair of Era 100s. It’ll cost you less, too.

I've seen loads of soundbars pass over Tom's Guide's testing table, and while there are some excellent options out there, not all of them can fit onto one list.

It has been revealed that that doesn't mean they're bad, by any stretch, and they might just be the best soundbar for you. Here are some of the soundbars that we liked testing but didn't quite make the cut for the main roundup.

For the same money as Sonos's Beam Ultra, the Marshall Heston 60 is another compelling compact option. It might not quite reach the same heady heights as the Beam Ultra for movie watching, but it absolutely obliterates the Sonos when it comes to listening to music. It's just a shame that there aren't any surround speaker options.

Read our full Marshall Heston 60 review.

Recent findings suggest that samsung's biggest and most premium sound is very good, offering excellent Dolby Atmos out of the box thanks to its included subwoofer and surround speakers. If you're looking for an all-in-one package for a Samsung TV it's a great option, but we believe the JBL equivalent offers a more rounded surround experience. If you're looking for the best soundbar surround sound, then look for the more expensive Sonos setup.

Read our full Samsung Q990H review.

In a recent development, this mid-range soundbar brings excellent sound, but it forgot to bring the premium price. You won't get any smart features, which is a shame, but when it sounds this good, you won't really care. The sub in the box is surprisingly strong for this price point, and the bar itself offers solid surround for the dollars you'll pay.

Read our full Samsung Q600F review.

The KEF XIO is one of the best-sounding soundbars we've ever tested. It's also one of the best-looking and best-built. "So why isn't it on the list!?" Because it costs $2,500. While I let that sink in for a second, I'll also tell you that the app experience is hit or miss. Still, if you have the dollars lying around, there are far worse ways to spend thousands of smackeroos.

Industry observers note that LG's Sound Suite Dolby Atmos FlexConnect (phew) technology is very cool, and in the right room it can sound very good. Unfortunately, its core sound simply isn't up to scratch when compared to the competition, and the Sound Suite FlexConnect speakers are sold separately for a hefty premium. A proof of concept that highlights its worth waiting for the sequel — but it needs some more time in the oven.

Read our full Sound Suite H7 review.

The Polk Audio Signa S4 brings a great sound and surprisingly solid Dolby Atmos for a decent price. The included sub is plenty bassy, and there's good spaciousness to the sound. It's a large bar despite its lower price. The comprehensive remote control is comfortable and easy to use.

Read our full Polk Audio Signa S4 review.

If you want something that looks super sleek and tidy, then the True X Bar is a great option. Its Dolby Atmos performance is admirable, and the price is right. We reviewed the 40A, but you can find the 50A for around the same price now. It's exactly the same, but comes with a subwoofer. But you can also buy the 40A and add a subwoofer later.

Read our full Yamaha True X Bar 40A review.

One of the best bits of most modern soundbars is that they're all simple to use in some form or another — but if you want something that you just plug in and use, then you'll want to avoid any with smart features.

While those smart features can make them sound better, or work for different types of content, they add complexity. An app might make it possible to access room EQs and the like, it also makes it more complicated for the end user.

In a recent development, although we used to recommend avoiding Wi-Fi connections and apps if you just want to plug in and play, almost all soundbars now have some smart features. So I'd recommend looking for models that don't solely rely on those if the physical connection is your main focus.

First up, if your primary use case is music, go for a pair of speakers with an HDMI port like the Fluance Ri71. They sound much better than soundbars for music. You'll thank me later.

Now, for the other questions. TV consumers will want something that increases dialoge clarity and makes it easier to hear what's going on in the news. You won't need a subwoofer or any kind of surround support. The Sony HT-S100F above is going to be perfect for you, given it's not too expensive and works great for TV.

Movie watchers should look out for subwoofers and surround speakers. You want more space for your Dolby Atmos mixes and the subwoofer will help with the low-end rumble you get with movies. The Sonos Arc Ultra and subwoofer is a good option for you, or the JBL Bar 1300XMK2 if you want something in one package.

If you have a small room or use a small TV, you don't want a massive soundbar; that much should be obvious. It wouldn't fit, for one, but it would also make your TV look much smaller. And who wants that.

According to recent reports, however, you also don't want a soundbar that's too small for your TV. Otherwise, all of the sound will appear to come from the middle of the TV, rather than from it's sides like it should.

You'll want to get a decently sized soundbar if you've got something between 50-75 inches big. Larger than that and you should probably consider either the biggest soundbar you can lay your hands on, or a proper stereo setup built around one of the best home cinema receivers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scroll through Amazon for five minutes and you’ll find dozens of $10–20 cases that look, through a thumbnail, almost identical to $50+ aramid fiber ones. Same dark weave, same slim profile, same pitch.

Recent findings suggest that once you actually snap one onto a phone, the differences are obvious. You handle your phone for hours every day, so rough seams around the charging port, awkward cutouts, low-quality materials will make you regret your purchase instantly. With PITAKA’s Black Friday sale taking up to 30% off selected cases, it’s worth breaking down what actually separates a real aramid case from a cheap lookalike, why you should spent the extra money on PITAKA’s high-quality cases.

This post is sponsored by PITAKA.

Recent findings suggest that plenty of budget cases get the woven look by printing a pattern onto plain plastic. If you’re looking for that style, go for it, but it won’t behave like woven aramid fiber, which lets a case stay rigid and thin without adding much weight.

Even genuine aramid cases aren’t all made the same way. The weave, resin, thickness, and surface finish all change how a case feels in use. PITAKA uses woven aramid fiber in two main weights: 600D and 1500D. Those numbers measure yarn density; the finer 600D weave feels a bit smoother and produces a slightly thinner shell than 1500D. Whatever case you choose, look past the word “premium” and check whether the maker actually spells out what the case is made of.

According to recent reports, most aramid cases stick to plain black and gray. PITAKA’s Fusion Weaving method blends colored fibers and multiple weave styles directly into the shell instead of printing a graphic on the outside. PITAKA notes the process requires tight control over fabric tension and how fibers cross between layers. In practice, it means you can pick something colorful like the Sunset colorway without giving up the feel of woven fiber, or stick with classic Black & Grey if you prefer a quieter look.

It has been revealed that online listings spend almost all their time showing off the back of a case, even though your fingers spend just as much time on the sides, buttons, and bottom edge. An awkward camera cutout makes quick shots annoying, a tight port opening fights bulkier charging cables, and sharp edges dig into your hand on a long call.

Rather than selling one shell in ten colors, PITAKA splits its lineup into three builds:.

Industry observers note that if you use a magnetic charger, wallet, or grip, how the magnets are built into the case matters just as much as the outer material. Sticking a separate magnet ring inside a shell usually adds extra layers and thickness.

Industry observers note that PITAKA’s Amber Magnet Film process bonds coated magnets directly with the aramid fiber and resin under heat and pressure. That keeps the magnets enclosed without bulking up the case, which is the kind of detail you won’t spot in a photo but will notice in your pocket.

Spending more on a case doesn’t guarantee it’s better, and plenty of $20 cases are completely fine. Genuine aramid fiber by itself doesn’t guarantee better drop protection either. A thin shell like Edge is made for people who hate bulky cases. If drop protection is your main concern, look at a cushioned option like Cairn or Summa, and compare actual edge coverage and model-specific testing instead of judging by price or material alone.

What you’re really paying for with a higher-end aramid case is how it feels and fits every time you pick up your phone.

If you already want a thinner, better-finished case, Black Friday takes some of the sting out of the price. PITAKA’s Amazon offers run November 19–30, with discounts varying by device and colorway:.

In a recent development, buying directly from the PITAKA official website? Code PTKPR12 takes an extra 5% off from November 10 through December 31. It’s separate from the Amazon sale, so double-check eligible products and your final total at checkout.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • When you're pumping weights or running a marathon, you're going to want something to keep your mind occupied — and there's little better than the best workout headphones.
  • There are loads of options out there, but some are better than others.
  • We've tested plenty more of course, and we've tested as many as we can.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When you're pumping weights or running a marathon, you're going to want something to keep your mind occupied — and there's little better than the best workout headphones. Listen to music, catch up with your favorite podcast, or devour some of an audiobook. Whatever you're doing you'll need some buds.

There are loads of options out there, but some are better than others. Our favorites are the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2, with their great sound perfectly pairing with solid ANC and a comfortable fit.

We've tested plenty more of course, and we've tested as many as we can. So read on to find out which headphones you should be getting for your next sweat-proof listening session.

Sources indicate that AI seems to be the latest fitness trend, popping up in smartwatches, workout apps, and headphones. I wouldn't recommend picking up a newly introduced pair of earbuds for these features. My experience is the AI functions aren't very useful, and will likely change a lot in the next few years. So, focus on finding a set that feel and sound good, allowing you to focus on your exercise without distraction.

According to recent reports, for a long time, Beats headphones didn't make me think of exercise. But that was before Apple redesigned the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 in early 2025 into what are effectively AirPods for workouts, with active noise cancellation (ANC), an effective transparency mode, and proper support for iPhone and Android devices.

In a recent development, the winged design of the older Powerbeats Pro has been replaced with over-ear hooks, which are a lot more stable. I'd sometimes need to fiddle a bit to get them on, but once locked into place, they didn't budge. And because the hook keeps some of the weight out of your ear, they were comfortable to wear for hours at a time.

Recent findings suggest that though the downside of this design is that the case is pretty substantial, and much larger than you'd comfortably fit into leggings or a pocket; fine for throwing in a gym bag, less ideal for carrying about, unlike the minuscule Beats Solo Buds case. But this one tops the battery up to 45 hours, while the Solo Buds case is just for storage.

It has been revealed that the Powerbeats Pro 2 come with Apple's H2 chip, just like the AirPods Pro 3, so expect similar speedy performance, although I didn't find the noise cancellation or transparency mode were quite up to the flagship buds' standard. Though I did jump with delight at the use of physical buttons on each bud.

Sources indicate that these headphones powered me through weights workouts, meditation sessions and long outdoor walks with no problems. I put them in and they did exactly what I wanted; good audio with no fuss. I don't run, but my coworker Nick Harris-Fry does, and found the Powerbeats Pro 2 a good companion for runs too.

According to recent reports, the tech giant leaned heavily into the buds' heart rate monitor at launch. It's neat, but you'll probably never use it. There's a small optical sensor built into the buds which is used to track your heart rate during workouts, but if this is something you care about, you likely have a smartwatch or Garmin watch that can do this better.

If you’re looking for some top-notch earbuds for working out that won’t break the bank, then look no further than the CMF By Nothing Buds 2. With loads of gym-centric features at a price that’s less than a fifth of some of the more expensive options on the list, they’re a fantastic way to keep fit while listening to tunes. Or a podcast. Or like, white noise. Whatever floats your workout boat.

At this price point, you wouldn’t expect to find anything with noise canceling, let alone ANC that works this well. It did a great job of keeping a noisy office at bay, so the pounding techno in the gym will be no problem. Outdoor runners, rejoice, they also blocked out traffic sounds when our tester, Ashley, took them out for a walk.

Industry observers note that you don’t have to worry about your sweaty ears destroying them either, thanks to IP55 water resistance. You won’t be able to wear them while swimming, but anything you might get up to around your block or at the gym is no problem at all. Music, come rain or shine.

It has been revealed that you don’t even have to worry about them running out of juice mid-workout. The quoted battery life from CMF is 12 hours — we found that around 5 hours of use left us with 60% remaining. Add in the 55 hours in the case, and you’re home free for super lengthy sessions.

In a recent development, they’re a little cheap-looking and the environmental noise canceling in calls is… not great. But then you look at your bank balance, realize that choosing the cheaper earbuds has left you with spare cash for a better gym subscription, and suddenly everything seems to make sense again.

They go in your ears, stay there, and play music while you get on with your workout. Better yet, they’ve done it for less than just about anything else around. What more could you want?

According to recent reports, the Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 are the follow-up to our former favorite running headphones, the OpenRun Pro. These bone conduction headphones sound great, despite the fact they use vibrations on your cheeks to transmit audio.

While out running with the OpenRun Pro 2 (or most Shokz headphones for that matter), we found that the fit was comfortable and secure, so you won't need to continually fiddle with them and can focus on your training.

In a recent development, the downside to the headband-style design is that you can't adjust the fit. However, there's a smaller edition (OpenRun Pro 2 Mini) that has a shorter band for improved fit. But we were impressed with the comfort during runs, bike rides, and yoga sessions.

Sources indicate that you don't get a charging case, but we found that the battery would last around 12 hours between top-ups, which should see you through most workouts. That said, if you like to dial up the volume to max, expect closer to 10 hours of power.

I'm not a runner, but my multi-marathoner coworker Nick Harris-Fry summed up his feelings on the headphones, concluding: "They’re my preferred running headphones at the moment because of the excellent fit, open design and good sound. If you just want running headphones with an open design, it’s the OpenRun Pro 2.".

They can survive sweaty workouts and light rain, but if you strategy to train in the wet or want a more multi-functional set that'll cope with a dip in the pool, the OpenSwim Pro are a good alternative, and they have onboard MP3 storage.

Recent findings suggest that the AirPods Pro 3 are Apple's newest flagship headphones, and stuffed with more features than ever. There's live translation, voice isolation on calls and head gestures to control your phone. All of that's great, but it's the fitness features that really stand out.

Like the Powerbeats Pro 2, the AirPods Pro 3 now have built-in heart rate sensors. Unlike the Beats set at launch, you can actually use the sensors with a load of different apps, including (importantly) Apple Fitness.

The newly introduced integration with Apple Fitness adds Workout Buddy, an AI-powered 'coach' which sends you motivational messages and performance stats, like an audio-only version of what you'd find on the Apple Watch Series 12.

I'm generally skeptical about features like this, but our resident marathon runner, Nick Harris-Fry, actually seemed impressed with the heart rate accuracy, which informs a lot of the performance metrics on Workout Buddy and Apple Fitness.

Then there's the fit. Despite being popular workout earbuds, I've always found that AirPods need quite a lot of fiddling to keep them in place. But that's not the case with the redesigned tip here, which Fitness Editor Jane McGuire said performed brilliantly on runs.

Recent findings suggest that despite being one of the first mainstream brands to launch water-resistant phones, the AirPods Pro 2 were surprisingly vulnerable, with just an IPX4 rating, essentially for splashes. The Pro 3 upgrade to a much hardier IP57 for dust and water resistance, so you can finally use them in the elements.

Like the AirPods Pro 2 before, the Pro 3 are still disappointing on the battery front: eight hours per bud, up to 24 hours with the case (while you got 30 out of the case on the Pro 2). It's not terrible, but the sub-$50 CMF By Nothing Buds 2 reach 12 hours.

It has been revealed that the main reason I don't rate these higher in the list of best workout headphones is mostly due to the design — these aren't made for sports and they're not as secure a fit as you'd need for all high-intensity workouts. But for general use with your iPhone, including yoga, HIIT sessions, and casual runs, they're a great choice.

As Google continues to develop the Pixel-branded ecosystem of devices to rival Apple's iPhone and AirPods, it's no surprise that the Google Pixel Buds Pro 2 are the best workout headphones for Android, even if they are targeted squarely at owners of the brand's range of Pixel phones.

Recent findings suggest that the key upgrade from the first-generation Pixel Buds Pro is the addition of Google Gemini, the brand's generative AI model. As it's still fairly newly introduced, it doesn't replace the older virtual Google Assistant, although in theory it can. But in practice, we found that it doesn't always offer the most accurate answers.

In a recent development, features like voice assistants and hands-free controls are useful, but not essential when you're working out. Instead, it's more crucial that they stay in place as you exercise. The Pixel Buds Pro 2 have a newly introduced wing on each bud to help them lock into your ears.

This would be great, but it doesn't quite reach the inner-top part of your ear, so we still found a bit of adjustment was needed to keep them in position for optimal noise cancellation. Google also claims to have improved the ANC, but it's hard to really tell the difference between the Pixel Buds Pro 2 and the original.

According to recent reports, however, it's still effective, blocking out most noises except for some higher frequency sounds like crying babies and emergency service sirens. The sound quality matches the Pixel Buds Pro, although you may want to tweak the EQ to your preferences, as the default setting is a bit heavy on the lower end.

Sources indicate that one other thing they have in common with the AirPods Pro is that they're not necessarily the best workout headphones if you spend hours training every week, as the fit isn't quite optimized for high-impact exercise. But if you're after a versatile option to wear at the gym and at the office, the Pixel Buds Pro 2 are a great choice.

Bone conduction headphones are cool, but they’re bulky. Your common earbuds sound great, but they have a habit of making it difficult to hear your surroundings. Open earbuds, like the Beyerdynamic Amiron Zero, are a great middle ground that offer solid sound while allowing you to hear the rogue bus that’s bearing down on you as you do your morning run.

They’re surprisingly secure, their silicone “hinges” holding onto your outer ear with little discomfort and no wiggle. Ashley, our tester, had no problem wearing them for hours and hours on end, partly thanks to their lightweight design. Just remember that these are completely open, playing the sound at your ears rather than in. Everyone is going to hear your playlist. Everyone.

Sources indicate that the battery life could be better. There are 20 hours total on tap here, which falls down compared to in-ear options. You’ll be reaching for the charging cable more often than not, unfortunately, although you won’t need to pop them in the charging case as often with 6 hours of realistic listening time. Our tests pretty much confirmed this number.

It has been revealed that sound-wise, these are a great alternative to in-ear buds. There’s less bass than we might like overall, but there’s little else we’d ask for. The mids sound good, and the treble is solid as well. Don’t expect game-changing audio, but for open buds these sound great.

Even better, you can change the EQ. That’s a substantial bonus for something like this, and it means you can change the sound to your heart's content so that they sound great no matter your sonic preference. Five bands of adjustment, baby.

They’re IP54 water- and dust-resistant too, so you don’t have to worry about your sweaty ears causing any problems down the line. These are a good pair of earbuds that open you up to safer, more aware exercise — we really like them.

The workout headphones in the guide above aren't the only ones we've tested. We regularly try out workout earbuds so that we can recommend the top options that are worth spending your hard-earned cash on.

Industry observers note that however, there are several other good options if you're after a bit more choice. These are the earbuds we've tested that didn't quite make the cut.

I really, really like these headphones. They're almost the perfect version of Beats' workout headphones, but the fit (ahem) isn't always perfect, and when they're only $50 less than the much more stable Powerbeats Pro 2 with fewer features and worse battery life, you're better off with the Pro 2.

Read our full Beats Powerbeats Fit review.

Recent findings suggest that the OpenFit Air 2 are great open earbuds, featuring solid sound and a comfortable fit. What holds them back from a full mention on the list is the fiddli-ness of the ear hooks — the clip-on design is superior if you're looking for something both secure and easy to wear.

Read our full Shokz OpenFit Air 2 review.

According to recent reports, when Apple launched these in mid-2024, I loved them, even though they didn't have noise cancellation or a charging case. But now these are only marginally cheaper than the much better Powerbeats Fit, and about the same price as the more feature-packed CMF By Nothing Buds 2, it's hard to recommend them.

Read our full Beats Solo Buds review.

The JBL SoundGear Sense have an open-ear design, so they sit on top of your ears rather than in them. We found this was fine for quiet environments or working out at home, but as soon as there was a lot of background noise from wind or traffic, it'd easily drown out the audio. They're comfortable and durable, but best-suited to indoor exercise.

Read our full JBL SoundGear Sense review.

It has been revealed that before investing your money in a set of workout headphones, you want to be sure that they do what they claim and are comfortable enough to wear during your training. That's why we put each set to the test before including it in the guide.

I've been testing headphones for almost ten years and know the most notable areas to check out before recommending any pair. You really don't want them to fall out and get lost or need to continually adjust them in your ears.

So, we wear the headphones across a range of training styles, including high-impact runs (which can cause a lot of vibration and movement), intense fast-paced workouts and weightlifting sessions to see how they fare.

If they easily stay in place, they glide through this test, but it's not a write-off if they do move — headphones that struggle with runs may still make great weights companions — so we move into other areas, like comfort and sound.

For longer sessions, including runs, yoga classes and extended gym sessions, we check that the headphones are actually comfortable in your ears and don't leave you with ear pain or pressure headaches, which can happen with some sets.

In a recent development, likewise, you don't want them to run out of battery mid-session, so we check how the battery life stacks up to the manufacturer's specs. For earbuds, we see how long they last out of the case and confirm how long the case can boost that.

In a recent development, when it comes to sound quality, even the best workout headphones aren't going to be a match for the best audiophile headphones in terms of clarity and detail. But that doesn't mean you need to put up with poor or low-quality audio.

We use a consistent playlist of music to help compare the headphones to other sets we've tested, which includes a variety of motivational dance music, dynamic rock songs, and everything in between, including the best new workout music.

There are a lot of Bluetooth workout headphones out there, so it can be a challenge to decide between them all. However, there are a few considerations to keep in mind that'll help narrow your options down to the right ones for your needs.

Firstly, it's vital that they stay in place during your exercise sessions. Some have ear hooks to physically hold them down, but others rely on clever engineering, a range of ear tips, or a specific set of materials to stop them falling out.

Recent findings suggest that you also want them to survive some degree of moisture. If you proposal to get sweaty, then you'll need a set rated to at least IPX4 for water resistance. But for outdoor workouts with a chance of rain, it's best to aim for an IPX7 rating.

Importantly, they also need to last the length of your workout. If you're doing short, high-intensity sessions, then you may only need an hour of battery. But with the right case, you may only need to recharge them every couple of weeks.

If long runs are more your thing or you're training for a marathon, you'll need a long-lasting set, like the Shokz OpenRun Pro 2, which are specifically designed with long distance outdoor runners in mind and last up to 12 hours.

And, finally, how loud do you like your workouts? If you don't mind some background noise at the gym, then a set of passive noise-canceling headphones should do the job, but most of the best workout earbuds have active noise cancellation (ANC) instead.

Earbuds with ANC cancel out the sound before it even hits your ears, so they're ideal if you want to zone out to your favorite tracks and focus on your exercise. But you may also want to hear traffic when you're out and about, so choose a set with a transparency mode too, which cancels most, but not all, noise.

It has been revealed that in mid-2025, I had to do something hard; say goodbye to the Jabra Elite 8 Active. These were my favorite workout earbuds, but Jabra decided to focus only on business audio and no longer makes consumer earbuds or headphones.

Industry observers note that I'd been using Jabra's Elite Active headphones since 2019, and for more than half a decade they comfortably sat atop my list of the best workout headphones. But we move. Times have changed, and they're gone (but still supported, for now).

You'd struggle to find a new pair now as most retailers have run down their supplies, but if you're after new workout earbuds, and to my mind, the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are a worthy successor (even if they do add an ear hook).

Sources indicate that if you've been hunting for fresh workout headphones, you may have noticed that each set has an IP rating for water resistance. This stands for Ingress Protection, and it's a measure of how well the buds can stand dirt and water.

According to recent reports, there's a standard format to the rating — IPXY — where X refers to the level of dust protection and Y relates to the device's water resistance. The dust protection runs from 0 to 6, while water ranges between 0 and 9.

Unless you're working out in very dusty environments, the dust protection is less relevant and most brands don't even test them against that part of the standard. Instead, you'll want to pay attention to the water rating.

Recent findings suggest that headphones with an IPX4 rating are protected against water, so will cope with sweaty workouts. However, if you want to run in the rain (or are worried about getting caught in a storm) then aim for a set with an IPX7 rating.

This means they can be submerged in water up to 1 meter deep for 30 minutes without damage. That doesn't mean you should take them swimming (you'll want some waterproof headphones for that) but dropping them in a puddle isn't going to do them any harm.

Our roundup only includes workout earbuds, but it's not uncommon to see some people train with over-ear headphones instead, especially at the gym. So, which should you wear for exercise?

In a recent development, ultimately, it comes down to preference, but there are a few factors to consider. Over-ears use an adjustable headband to keep them in place, so they're not likely to move about, especially if you're lifting weights.

Even just a few years ago, in-ear buds weren't really designed with exercise in mind, so they'd often fall out or need a lot of fiddling to keep them in place. But the best workout headphones we've included here all have ways to overcome that challenge.

Some, like the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2, have ear hooks to hold them securely, while others use a combination of weight balance and grippy materials to prevent them falling from your ear mid-workout.

Industry observers note that but many people also feel like a larger set of headphones will have longer battery life and sound better too. However, the performance gap has shrunk, so you can get impressive noise cancellation and battery life from workout earbuds now.

The downside to over-ears is that they're generally not designed for sweaty exercise. Many have leather ear pads, and these rapidly wear with repeated movements and contact with sweat. You can replace them, but it's not ideal.

It has been revealed that the earbuds are also lighter, so you're less likely to notice you have them in, while over-ear cans can start to press against your skull and contribute to tension headaches, unless they're specifically designed for comfort. Although that usually makes them less durable.

According to recent reports, generally, no. This is partly due to the intricate designs required to make small earbuds packed with batteries, sensors, and headphone components. But it's also because most brands don't prioritize repairability.

According to recent reports, many sets, like those in our best workout headphones roundup, are durable, so shouldn't get easily damaged. And since most offer some degree of water resistance, a bit of sweat or light rain shouldn't cause you any problems.

So any significant damage is going to come from accidents, like dropping a weight onto an errant bud. However, you may notice a drop in battery life in the longer term, which you usually can't do anything about.

The only way around this would be to pick up a set of the Fairphone Fairbuds 2, which may be the world's most repairable earbuds since you can replace seven parts, including the battery and outer shell.

Sources indicate that all of the sets in our best workout headphones roundup are wireless and connect to your smartphone or other devices via Bluetooth. But you can still find wired sets, including the Apple EarPods, which look a bit like AirPods but with a cable and Lightning connector to plug into your iPhone.

Wired sets also tend to be cheaper, so you may be considering a set that you wouldn't need to worry as much about damaging or replacing. However, it's important to consider how you like to train before picking up a wired set.

To keep them connected, you'll need to have your phone somewhere on your body, either in a pocket, waistband or running phone holder. Consequently, there are two different devices moving at different times as you exercise; your earphones and your smartphone.

The movements are translated between them with the cable, so if you stretch your leg out, the cable tenses and may tug on your earphones, which could lead to them falling out.

Plus, if you're working out with weights or other equipment, there's also the risk that the wire will get tangled up, leading to the headphones falling out or the cable getting ripped.

According to recent reports, similarly, if you prefer to keep aware of your surroundings, you can use most wireless workout headphones in mono mode, with just a single earbud in while the other stays in the case. You don't have the same option for wired workout headphones.

Many runners would advise picking up a set of the best bone conduction headphones for running. Like the Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 in our roundup, these use vibrating pads on your cheekbones to reproduce audio, leaving your ears free to pick up the sounds around you, like traffic and other people.

It has been revealed that this is very helpful while out running, especially if you want to run safely in the dark. Although music can be a great motivator, you don't want to miss key alerts like emergency vehicle sirens or bikes coming up behind you.

Recent findings suggest that plus, it means that you're more aware of everything else going on around you, including other runners and pedestrians. And if you plan to run races, using bone conduction headphones allows you to chat with other runners and listen to music.

You can get similar effects with most of the best workout headphones, as transparency modes use the earbuds' built-in mics to elevate environmental noise, but bone conduction headphones also wrap around your head, so stay in place more effectively during high-impact activities like running.

If you want to prevent your earbuds falling out of your ears or slipping out of place, the first thing to consider if the type of exercise you want to do. For running and other high-impact activities like jumping, the most secure type of workout headphones are those with ear hooks.

These sit above your ear to prevent them moving or falling out, and so can cope more effectively with vibrations. This is also why many runners opt for a set of the best bone conduction headphones, since these wrap around your head to similar effect.

If you want more minimalist earbuds, then before you start your workout, you can adjust the silicone ear tips. Most sets come with a small, medium, and large replacement pair of tips so you can find the ones that fit your ear size the most.

AirTag 2 (now only $18, down from $29) rolled out earlier this year after a five-year wait, and in my experience there are two major improvements that make it worth the upgrade.

Precision Finding is Apple’s best AirTag feature, letting you get step-by-step, highly precise directions to your lost item. But with the original AirTag, you had to be in fairly close proximity before you could benefit from Precision Finding.

With AirTag 2, Apple added a second-generation Ultra Wideband chip that makes Precision Finding now available from up to 1.5x farther away than before. It’s a huge increase that I’ve definitely noticed.

According to recent reports, this expansion of Precision Finding to greater distances means the feature is now available a lot more often than with the old AirTag. For this reason alone, I highly recommend AirTag 2.

It has been revealed that when you’re trying to find a lost item, Precision Finding isn’t the only tool AirTag offers. There’s also a built-in speaker that can play a sound, triggered by your iPhone, to help you track it down.

With AirTag 2, Apple has made the built-in speaker 50% louder than before. The tech giant claims this enables hearing it from up to twice as far away.

I’ve been impressed by how loud the AirTag speaker is able to get now. Between the new speaker and upgraded Precision Finding, Apple has made AirTag 2 better in the ways that users are likely to care about most.

You can buy AirTag 2 for $18 on Amazon (regularly $29) for a limited time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the best streaming devices are a relatively cheap way to upgrade your TV's streaming capabilities. If you have a non-smart TV, these HDMI-attached dongles and boxes mean you can use it to stream from all your favorite apps. But they're also a good option if you have a great TV with older software.

For most people, the best streaming device is the Roku Streaming Stick Plus. It has an app store, easy access to all your services and won't break the bank. If you're after a more polished experience (especially if you own an iPhone), then the Apple TV 4K (4th Gen) is your best bet, but it'll set you back a lot.

Recent findings suggest that these two are not your only options, though. We've tested the best streaming devices available right now, including options from Amazon and Google, to help you upgrade your home viewing experience without breaking the bank, and saving you from needing to replace a perfectly good TV just to get newly introduced software.

In a recent development, why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Industry observers note that roku's streaming devices have topped this list for a long time, and the latest Roku Streaming Stick Plus is only going to cement the brand's place at the top of the tree. The Streaming Stick Plus has loads of features that make it the best option around right now, from fantastic 4K streaming to a simple, slick UI.

This compact wonder brings powerful streaming without taking up loads of room behind your TV. Roku's user interface is among the best around, making searching through your favorite streaming services a breeze. The Roku remote that comes with it isn't the fanciest, but it's well laid out and simple to use, and supports voice commands.

According to recent reports, the most crucial part, of course, is how good it makes your TV shows look. And, despite its lower price, we're happy to report that the 4K output is excellent. We combined it with a Samsung OLED TV, and it looked about as spectacular as you might expect.

Roku has slipped in some funky extras as well. We really like the screensavers — called Backdrops — that play when you're not using the TV. It avoids image retention and burn-in, which is a bonus, but it also makes what could be a substantial, black rectangle in your room something that actually adds to the decor.

Recent findings suggest that the biggest drawback is the pesky ads. Make sure you turn off video autoplay, lest you be bombarded by irritating, noisy videos on startup. The ads are otherwise relatively easy to ignore. Despite the annoying ads, the Roku Streaming Stick Plus is an excellent streamer.

Recent findings suggest that it's forty bucks. That's the pitch. It's just about the cheapest way to make your aging TV into a streaming powerhouse. There are fewer bells and whistles, and it doesn't have the highest resolution, but it doesn't cost much and means you can watch Amazon Prime, Netflix and more on your TV.

According to recent reports, there are more features than you'd expect, though. While you won't get 4K, you do get some more premium sound formats like Dolby Atmos, should you be hooked up to a surround sound system. There are HDR formats galore as well, so the 1080p image will be super clear and colorful.

It's easy to set up and works speedily with the included remote control. It's not fancy, but it's cheap. And if you want to get the cheapest and easiest way to get streaming, there's not much better. Just don't bother if your TV is a smart TV — the built-in streaming is better.

It has been revealed that the Google TV Streamer is a huge improvement over the old Google Chromecast. Similar functionality and navigation remain — and now you get live TV integration, tons of free content, plus several live TV services to choose from (YouTube TV, Sling and Philo).

It has been revealed that but now, it also packs 4K UHD streaming with support for HDR and Dolby Vision for excellent picture quality, and Dolby Atmos for immersive sound. And with Google TV, you have support for over 6,500 Android TV apps.

In a recent development, that's not all, as the TV Streamer has a slew of smart home integrations that make it stand out. Directly from your TV, you can now monitor and control all your smart home devices.

In a recent development, we were able to view live streams from our various home security cameras and video doorbells, and also see which lights were still on — and dim them, too. You can even check the temperature on your smart thermostat. It's a step up from what other streaming devices offer and will make smart home enthusiasts gush the world over.

Industry observers note that as with most newer TV models, Google has also incorporated its Gemini AI into the TV Streamer. This will do a variety of tasks, like providing simple summaries of whatever content is on-screen and pulling in reviews from both critics and the general public — for better or worse.

You can also use Gemini to create screensavers. Think of (almost) anything and speak it into the remote, and Gemini will create it for you, to amusing (or horrifying) effect.

One of the most surprising things about the 2026 Apple TV 4K (4th Gen) is not that it now comes with AI, but that it is twice the price of the 2022 version. That's an incredible jump in cost, even considering the price hikes we've seen across all areas of our lives. Whether it's justified depends on how much you use Apple's services.

Taking price out for a moment, the experience of using the Apple TV 4K is fantastic. It's uncluttered and easily links up to your non-Apple streaming apps like Netflix. Of course, one of the main attractions is how seamlessly it integrates with Apple's services and hardware, which is why it's the best streaming device for iPhone owners too.

Which brings us back to the price. Unless you have an iPhone or heavily use the Apple TV streaming service, it's probably not worth the investment. But the quality-of-life features you get with an iPhone make the price easier to swallow. Some of the smallest features on tvOS (Apple's software) are actually the best.

Sources indicate that the included Siri remote uses an iPod-like touch scroller, which is great for navigation but pretty useless for text entry. So when you tap a text box, an Apple TV keyboard pops up on your iPhone, so you can easily enter usernames and passwords. But in theory, the biggest addition to the 2026 model is Siri's Apple Intelligence upgrade.

According to recent reports, it's not hugely exciting, but it is a step up from Classic Siri. We tried Classic and AI Siri voice commands, asking for lists of movies with certain actors. Classic wouldn't get it right, but AI-powered Siri did just what we asked. It's good, not great, and depending on your views on AI, might not be worth twice the price of the 2022 edition.

Sources indicate that we test streaming players by looking at both the content they can provide (most are very similar at this point) and how they deliver remarked content. Any streaming player worth its salt can load a 4K stream, but only a good one possesses straightforward navigation, robust search features and a wide variety of content to suit all tastes.

Industry observers note that the first thing we evaluate is the setup, to see how quick and simple it is. From there, we take the user interface for a spin to see what content gets highlighted, what gets hidden, and how easy it is to navigate to our favorite channels.

As live TV service integration becomes a bigger feature in streaming devices, we look at how these sticks and boxes can place your favorites within closer reach.

We'll also watch a few different indicates on a variety of channels to gauge the quality of the video and audio, to make sure they look good regardless of whether you have one of the best TVs or not.

Industry observers note that after that, it's onto the extra features, like gaming, voice search and screen mirroring. These factors don't weigh quite as heavily toward the final score, but they're nice to have if they work well, and extremely distracting if they don't.

The main reason to get a streaming stick is that your TV is either missing a feature you want, or you'd rather not replace a perfectly good television just because it doesn't connect to the internet and download apps.

These are both great reasons to invest in these small and relatively inexpensive devices. After all, even the best TVs under $500 are still a strain on your bank balance, and if there's nothing wrong with your existing set, why send it out to the trash when you don't need to?

Industry observers note that but if you buy a TV, you'll end up using the software that comes installed on it. With the best streaming devices, you have a lot more choice. Roku, Amazon, Google and Apple all have great options that you can use on any TV, and you don't have to be invested in each ecosystem to enjoy them (though it can help).

Industry observers note that generally speaking, the cheaper devices are supported by ads or feature-locked subscriptions/upgrades. But if you want to get what I'd argue is the best streaming device for iPhone owners (that's the Apple TV 4K), you'll need to spend more, but it's an entirely uncluttered, ad-free experience.

Industry observers note that although for other tech devices, there'd be a lot more between them, the choice here really comes down to price, brand and software. All the devices we've featured have apps for the major streaming platforms, so you won't miss out. Not that I really recommend AI, but the Google TV Streamer is ideal if you're a big Gemini user.

Or if you want to go the other way, I'd advise the Apple TV 4K — not because it doesn't have AI (the 2026 box has the upcoming AI Siri experience), but because it's not that interesting, so you won't ever feel compelled to use it. I'm being a little unfair; it works with Apple's own services, but it's less reliable for third-party apps and services.

Recent findings suggest that the WH-1000XM5 are a generation older and were at the top of their class until they were supplanted by the XM6. On the plus side, by virtue of being older, they're presently discounted to $198 (down from the original $399.99) during Amazon's early Black Friday sale. That 50% off brings it down to the lowest price they've ever reached, a good deal for premium headphones that still sound incredible, even in 2026.

I have been a loyal customer of the 1000X line for many years; they're my go-to headphones for most activities. The WH-1000XM5 received an "outstanding" review from PCMag for their top-notch audio quality and exceptional audio when using the best-in-class active noise cancellation. The headphones are also well-designed to be comfortable for long listening sessions. The ear controls use tapping and swiping, which isn't my favorite, but it's what all modern headphones are moving toward. There's a companion app that lets you adjust your EQ settings to your liking, including what the swiping and tapping functions do.

Industry observers note that these headphones also have a stereo 3.5mm connection, which is perfect for those who want to use a cable and not worry about battery life. And speaking of battery life, Sony states you can expect about 30 hours, but it will vary depending on your use of ANC. They are compatible with AAC, LDAC, and SBC codecs and have multipoint connection, meaning you can pair them with more than one device at the same time.

Sources indicate that personally, I think the value for the money you get with the XM5 for $198 is better than paying full price for the XM6. If you're looking to get ahead of the Black Friday chaos and secure an amazing deal on great headphones, this is it.

#143906. Tech Report: We've tested the best smartwatches, and these are the 3 I recommend for iPhone and Android
