Tech Report: We've tested the best smartwatches, and these are the 3 I recommend for iPhone and Android

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2699 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the best smartwatch is almost always the one that works with your phone.
  • Sources indicate that one of the remaining holdouts is Amazfit, which launched the excellent Active 3 Premium that works on iPhone and Android.
  • It's incredible value, but if you're looking for the closest integration you can get with your phone or smart features like emergency or health alerts, then I'd recommend the Apple Watch Series 12 (iPhone) or Google Pixel Watch 5 (Android) right now.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the best smartwatch is almost always the one that works with your phone. Over the past few years, brands have moved away from universal compatibility and toward platform-specific watches that will only work if you use a particular phone.

Sources indicate that one of the remaining holdouts is Amazfit, which launched the excellent Active 3 Premium that works on iPhone and Android. It's half the price of Apple or Google's watches, but you wouldn't know it from its impressive fitness tracking features.

It's incredible value, but if you're looking for the closest integration you can get with your phone or smart features like emergency or health alerts, then I'd recommend the Apple Watch Series 12 (iPhone) or Google Pixel Watch 5 (Android) right now.

In a recent development, why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

In a recent development, the Amazfit Active 3 Premium is the smartwatch I recommend for most people, and not just because it works with whichever phone you have. It's a fantastic fitness-tracking watch that easily holds its own against the Apple Watch Series 12 and Google Pixel Watch 5, without locking you to a specific platform or phone.

It is also incredible value — coming in at around half the price of the two flagship watches — and all the features are free with no subscription (unless you need Zepp Aura, the sleep-focused AI wellness app that generates audio to relax you). It has offline maps, tracks more than 170 activities, and comes with built-in GPS.

Industry observers note that it has a smaller footprint (wristprint?) than many other smartwatches, with a 1.3-inch display, compared to the 1.77- or 1.96-inch Apple Watch Series 12. It's not a huge amount on paper, but it makes a massive difference, as it felt smaller and less noticeable on our wrist. It's a shame it doesn't come in a few more vibrant colors, though.

While you don't get the smarts of Apple and Google's watches (emergency alerts, on-watch calls, third-party apps), fitness and activity tracking is where the Active 3 Premium really shines, with metrics to rival the best Garmin watches, like heart rate, blood oxygen, stress levels, cycle tracking, sleep quality and skin temperature.

The data all syncs to your phone, and you can view it and get insights in the Zepp app, available for Android and iPhone. If you ever used a Fitbit before the Google takeover, the Zepp app is the closest thing to that now-gone experience; easy to understand, straightforward to use, and guides you through all the different metrics.

This is particularly helpful if you're just getting into running, as the running features on the Active 3 Premium are almost as detailed as those you'd find on Garmin watches, yet everything is explained clearly, even for more complex topics like your lactate threshold and ground contact time, which assess how your foot strikes the floor.

Amazfit says that the Active 3 Premium should last 12 days between charges. Like most other smartwatches, that doesn't work out in the real world; we found that it'd generally last just over a week or eight days. That's down a bit on the spec, but still miles ahead of the 24-hour battery life on the Apple Watch Series 12.

Sources indicate that apple, Google and Samsung refresh their watches every year. Normally, these are pretty small upgrades, so I often recommend buying the previous year's model. But not with the Apple Watch Series 12. For the first time in almost half a decade, Apple has given the watch a pretty big health-tracking update.

Industry observers note that the most significant change is that there's a latest, more accurate heart rate sensor. This powers a few other changes, like the Readiness score you can get each day. This is something imported from other running watches and is a measure of how you've recovered after activity and how to improve the score.

I've tested watches with this kind of score and haven't found it that informative, but I know our resident runners find it particularly helpful when training for races. The improved sensors also allow for continuous heart rate monitoring (ie all day), which was previously limited to just during tracked workouts.

In a recent development, these practical and useful changes were only part of the Series 12 pitch. Apple also rolled out new AI Siri and a selection of 'helpful' AI-powered features, called Audio Intelligence. There are two (Live Rewind, Siri Recap), but both use the watch to capture speech around you and turn it into some form of recap.

In a recent development, live Rewind is arguably the least helpful and most invasive. It listens to conversations (privately on your phone) and allows you to rewind live conversations in case you miss a detail, like someone's name (in case you were unaware you could ask the person to repeat what they noted). Recap uses AI to summarize all that data into a journal-like, 'here's what happened today' note.

According to recent reports, honestly, these seem like gimmicks to me that very few people will ever use, and it normalizes surveillance. So, in case it wasn't clear, I wouldn't buy the watch for these and would jump into the settings to disable them. But in all other aspects, the Series 12 is the best Apple Watch you can buy right now and a worthy upgrade.

As with the Apple Watch, I wouldn't normally recommend the most recent version of the Google Pixel Watch, but this time I do think the Google Pixel Watch 5 is the better choice than the 4, but mostly because it's hard to find a newly introduced edition of the Pixel Watch 4 now that the Pixel Watch 5 exists.

Industry observers note that that doesn't mean I don't think the Pixel Watch 5 is a great smartwatch — it is — but it's a relatively modest upgrade this time around. But what you get for your money still makes it the best smartwatch for Android phones, especially if you own a Pixel device. And like Apple, it's the fresh health and safety features that are the headline.

Industry observers note that the Pixel Watch 5 includes Breathing Emergency Detection, which is a lot like 2024's Loss of Pulse Detection, which uses the watch's sensor data to look for signs of a breathing emergency and automatically requests 911 support or trusted contacts for help. These two, along with Fall/Crash Detection, Blood Pressure Trends, and Insulin Resistance Trends, form part of Google's new "Health Guardian" suite.

Technologically, it's impressive. But do I recommend you buy the watch for them? I don't think so. It's a reassuring fallback if you do have an emergency, but you can't say with certainty that they'll always work as intended when you need them to. And reviewers (including us) can't really test them to check either.

Sources indicate that what I like about the Pixel Watch range is that Google doesn't tie too many features exclusively to Pixel phones. The Pixel-exclusive features on the Watch 5 are: call screening, secure phone unlock, contact cards when someone calls you, and the ability to use your watch as a remote viewfinder for your phone's camera app.

Sources indicate that the newest watch has also retained my favorite feature: repairable screens and replaceable batteries. This isn't as easy as popping the back off, but it makes the Pixel Watch 5 the most repairable smartwatch you can buy right now. iFixit even rated it a near-perfect 9/10 for repairability, while the Apple Watch Series 12 scored just 4/10.

According to recent reports, it's not easy for me to praise Google (have you seen the Google Graveyard?), but it's a hugely positive move that saves you money in the long run and prevents otherwise good watches from going to the trash. But much of this was also true of the Pixel Watch 4, so if you can find a good deal on the older model, I'd go for that.

If you're after the best smartwatch for your phone, the three models I recommend above are going to cover most use cases, whichever phone you have. But there are a lot more smartwatches around right now.

In a recent development, not every model can be the best, but some come pretty close. If you need a few more options, these are the smartwatches I still think are worth your money, and may fill a need we didn't cover in the wearables from Amazfit, Apple or Google.

Last year's Apple Watch Series 11 is so close to the older Series 10 that it does make you wonder why Apple released it, but for the first time in many years, there was a bump in battery life from 18 hours on the Series 10 to 24 hours on the Series 11. If you can get a good discount, it's a great option, but the Series 12 is a much better watch for not much more.

Read our full Apple Watch Series 11 review.

According to recent reports, the Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 generates free wellbeing insights from your data. This is a neat upside, as many other brands charge for this. The (potential) downside is that you need a Samsung phone to access them all in the Samsung Health app. But it's more expensive than the Galaxy Watch 8, despite modest changes and the same display. The Pixel Watch 5 is a better option unless you really need the Samsung integration.

Read our full Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 review.

Apple didn't release a new budget watch in 2026, so the most recent is the 2025 SE 3. It's an excellent choice and has almost all the same features as the Series 10 and 11, minus some health-specific ones like ECG and blood oxygen monitoring. And like those models, it lacks the upgraded health sensors of the Series 12. If you can do without them, the SE 3 is a great value Apple Watch.

Read our full Apple Watch SE 3 review.

Industry observers note that the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is a useful update from the Ultra 3 with a redesigned, more accurate health sensor array and better battery life. It also comes with the same AI gimmicks as the Series 12. It's a good option if you need a larger, longer-lasting Apple Watch, but for most people, the Series 12 is the better (and cheaper) choice.

Read our full Apple Ultra 4 review.

In a recent development, the Withings ScanWatch Light is a stripped-back version of the hybrid ScanWatch 2 I wear every day. It doesn't have a large color screen and is missing features like calls and apps, but it can track your activity, heart rate and workouts. I love the ScanWatch 2, and the compromise to reduce the cost is that the Light drops the flagship watch's health features, like an ECG. Otherwise, this is an excellent fitness tracking watch that'll last several weeks between charges.

Read our full Withings ScanWatch Light review.

The CMF Watch 3 Pro is impressively cheap, retailing for less than most fitness trackers. It has a color display and two weeks of battery life; incredible at this price. But we found that step counts are inaccurate and the sleep tracking is unreliable. So I'd recommend the Amazfit Active 3 Premium instead.

Read our full Nothing CMF Watch 3 Pro review.

We reviewed the first Apple Watch more than a decade ago, and we've been testing the best smartwatches ever since. The devices have gotten more complex, last longer and have way more features now, but the core of our testing has remained the same: we wear the watches, just as you would, to see how they hold up in the real world.

Industry observers note that we look at how easy it is to set up, whether it has compatibility challenges with specific phones and spending hours poking around in the software, looking for settings, apps and other features that make the device worth your money. Over the years, these watches have transitioned from phone companions to health and wellbeing trackers.

Sources indicate that so we also focus on how these tools work, whether the tracking is accurate, how it compares to the competition and whether there's value in measuring what the tech giant claims you should. We wear the best smartwatches out on runs, during workouts, while sleeping and going about our day to see how they cope.

According to recent reports, over the past few years, brands have added more safety features to their watches, like irregular heartbeat notifications, sleep apnea alerts, crash and fall detection and hypertension alerts. These are things we can't practically test, so we can't verify that these work as intended or described.

In the U.S., health features are regulated by the FDA, so there is some degree of verification, but because we can't check that ourselves, I wouldn't recommend that you buy any of these watches specifically for these safety features. At the very least, they should be secondary to some other safety check.

In a recent development, it's not something you can predict, but sometimes a health concern does come along when you're testing a smartwatch. This happened to one of our writers — her Garmin watch alerted her to a potential heart problem she didn't know about, and that prompted her to go to the hospital to get checked out.

Before you go too far into your journey for a latest smartwatch, first you need to work out which ones will work with your phone. The Apple Watch only works with iPhones, and some Android-focused watches have features that are exclusive to specific phones (I'm thinking of offerings from Google and Samsung here).

There are plenty of options that'll work with both platforms, but they generally aren't the flagship models that get a lot of attention every summer and fall, like the watch I rate as the best smartwatch right now, the Amazfit Active 3 Premium. It's more of a fitness smartwatch, but it can do a lot of what the others can do for a lot less.

And that's one of the other big choices you have to make: do you want a fitness watch that has smartwatch features, or a smartwatch as a companion to your phone that can track your fitness? These sound similar — and they are — but the difference is how much of the focus is put on either the smartwatch or fitness features.

Fitness smartwatches evolved from the best fitness trackers, with larger displays and more sensors. The best smartwatches started life as Bluetooth-connected extensions of your phone and over time became devices that keep you connected to your digital life, even when you're away from your phone working out.

In a recent development, the Apple Watch Series 12 and Google Pixel Watch 5 are the best compromise between the two, but there are plenty of other options in our Also Consider section that also straddle that line or lean one way or the other. Though, if you need a cellular connection in your watch, those are pretty much limited to the flagship models.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google is rolling out newly introduced privacy settings for the Gemini app that will let you “keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.”.
  • Recent findings suggest that update 11/24: This upcoming setting is now widely rolling out.
  • It has been revealed that under “Help train generative AI models with,” you’ll find the upcoming “Chat content including text & attachments” setting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google is rolling out newly introduced privacy settings for the Gemini app that will let you “keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.”.

Recent findings suggest that update 11/24: This upcoming setting is now widely rolling out. On gemini.google.com, tap the settings gear icon to find a new “Gemini History” item at the very bottom. This opens myactivity.google.com/product/gemini with an On/Off dropdown.

It has been revealed that under “Help train generative AI models with,” you’ll find the upcoming “Chat content including text & attachments” setting. It’s enabled by default.

Your future chats won’t be used to train generative AI models, unless you provide feedback.

Training on “Audio and Gemini Live videos & screenshares” remains an opt-in preference.

Original 11/16: Gemini’s existing Keep Activity setting “controls how long your chats are saved and whether they are used to train generative AI models.”.

Google is now separating that preference into two latest options.

It has been revealed that this is huge. One of the major things Siri-AI users on iPhone like to point out is that while their assistant is a less capable portmanteau of Siri and Gemini, their queries are not used for AI training. Gemini on Android, on the other hand, offers the superior AI platform with the caveat that there is no way to opt out of training and still retain your chat history. Until now. Now users of Gemini on Android get the best of both worlds - the best of Google's AI models powering their AI experiences and their chat history siloed from AI training.

The first setting is called “History” and lets you “control how long your history is saved.” If disabled:.

“…future chats will be saved for around 2 months and used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its consumers, and the public, with help from human reviewers.”.

The duration is presently 24 hours for chat context, and 72 hours to help protect Google, users, and the public.

The second setting allows you to “separately control whether your chat content, including text and attachments, is used to train generative AI models.”.

With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.

If Keep Activity is at the moment off, the two “new settings will both be off.” These changes are rolling out over the “coming weeks,” and Google is notifying consumers via email.

Jesse Eisenberg is reflecting on his work in Hollywood and why he has a very different experience with fans in public than some other actors.

In a new interview with The New Yorker, the actor, director, writer, and producer of The Debut mentioned fans of his work are “mostly fine” when they see him in public, as his roles are not sexualized.

Industry observers note that eisenberg noted in the interview that he goes to the New York Public Library, where he writes scripts. When asked if people interrupt him when they recognize who he is, he told the publication, “People are mostly fine.” Related Stories News Jesse Eisenberg TV Series Produced By Peter Rice To Be Taken Out By A24 News Jesse Eisenberg Reveals Thoughts On 'The Social Reckoning' & Why He Turned Down Zuckerberg Role.

“It’s because there’s no sexuality to my work,” he added. “I think once the public is asked to want to sleep with a person onscreen, that person’s life is fundamentally different.” Watch on Deadline.

Eisenberg, who earned an Oscar nomination for his role in Aaron Sorkin’s The Social Network as Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg, recalled an interaction with a fan.

“I’d be out at a bar, and a drunk guy would say, ‘Hey, I love your website,’” he remarked. “And as I’m pretending to laugh, I’d just wish all of the oxygen would leave my lungs, and that I would collapse on the floor in front of this guy and show him what he’s doing to me.”.

Recent findings suggest that the actor didn’t return for the sequel, The Social Reckoning, and has been outspoken about his decision. Succession alum Jeremy Strong took on the role of Zuckerberg after Eisenberg declined.

Eisenberg’s The Debut opens in theaters on December 11, and the cast also includes Julianne Moore, Paul Giamatti, Halley Bailey, Colton Ryan, and Bernadette Peters, among others.

In a recent development, retailers and brands are churning out Black Friday deals, including the likes of Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, Samsung, and others. If you're a Sam's Club member, you have access to many Black Friday deals worth checking out, so I spent some time combing through their website and rounded up my favorite tech deals.

It has been revealed that the Bose SoundLink Flex SE is a portable Bluetooth speaker with an IP67 waterproof rating. The speaker even floats in the water, so you can bring it with you into the pool. While it doesn't offer full EQ customization in its companion app, the sound has rich bass depth and clear highs out of the box. It also features a speakerphone, allowing you to take calls and speak with it. It's light and portable, and the Bluetooth 5.3 supports multipoint connectivity and SBC, AAC, and aptX codecs. You can get the Bose 2nd Generation SoundLink Flex SE for $89 (originally $139).

Recent findings suggest that skullcandy makes fun speakers and headphones, although they're not designed for audiophiles (their sound signature is very bass-heavy). Their Skullcandy Stomp XL Max is their attempt at making a portable party speaker. It comes with two wireless mics, making it a great option for karaoke. It holds 12 hours of battery life (up to 20 hours with certain settings), has an IPX5 water resistance rating, and has LED lights that sync to the music. You can get it for $99 (originally $199).

Getting a soundbar can exponentially improve anyone's entertainment system, but a 5.1 system with rear speakers and a subwoofer takes it to the next level. The Samsung HW-Q65F 5.1 Channel Soundbar is $299 (originally $399), and it's a wireless setup that will keep the harmony of "too many cables" in the house. It supports Dolby Atmos and DTS Virtual:X to give you a 3D audio feel, and it has a dialogue feature that will let you hear the whispers.

Recent findings suggest that these kinds of sales are always a good time to upgrade laptops. If you're looking for a powerful computer that is well-rounded, consider the 16-inch HP OmniBook 7 Flip going for $699 (originally $899). This laptop comes with an Intel Ultra 5 processor, 512GB of SSD, and 16GB of RAM (which, honestly, is the minimum anyone should be buying in 2026).

Sources indicate that if you need a bigger screen, the 17.3-inch HP OmniBook 3 is a good choice for a bit less money at $649 (originally $999). It comes with an Intel Core Ultra 7 processor, 512GB of SSD, and 12GB of RAM. Part of the bigger screen means a bigger keyboard, so if you deal with numbers a lot, you'd likely appreciate the numeric pad.

If you want your laptop strictly for gaming, the ASUS TUF F16 Gaming laptop is $1,149 (originally $1,399). With an Intel Core 7 processor and the RTX 5060 graphics card, you'll be well set up to tackle heavy games. It comes with a 165Hz refresh rate, Advanced Arc Flow fans and vents to keep your machine cool, and 16GB DDR5 RAM to keep your loads short.

Gaming monitors can get expensive quickly, but you can get decent options on a budget. A great example is the 31.5-inch MSi gaming monitor selling for $129 (originally $179). It has a 250Hz refresh rate and a 1ms response time to make gaming smoother. There's also AMD FreeSync Premium to get rid of tearing and stuttering.

Budget TVs get big discounts during Black Friday, and the 58-inch Vizio QLED TV is one of them. You can get one for $178 (originally $298), and it supports Dolby Vision HDR for better color and contrast. The operating system is the Vizio OS, but of course, you can always change it with a TV dongle if you prefer a different one.

If you prefer to splurge for a better QLED but still get a good deal, the 65-inch Samsung QN90H QLED TV at $1,197.99 (originally $1,497.99) is a great option. It upscales lower-resolution pictures to 4K with AI. It works for gaming with its 144Hz refresh rate, and because the operating system is Tizen OS, it comes with Samsung TV Plus, which brings over 2,700 free channels. The TV also comes with Dolby Atmos, so you can hear audio with a 3D effect as the audio follows objects around the display.

Recent findings suggest that A 100-inch TV makes a statement: You take your entertainment system seriously. The 100-inch Vizio QLED TV is a budget-friendly option with a $300 discount, right now going for $1,198 (originally $1,498). This TV supports Dolby Vision HDR for more vivid images and has hundreds of free channels with the Vizio OS.

In a recent development, nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Sam Club's 2026 Black Friday sale runs from November 26 to November 29, 2026, starting online at 12:01 a.m. on Thanksgiving Day, but the deals start even earlier.

In a recent development, yes, you'll need to be a member to get the deals, but you can shop online without a membership with a 10% surcharge. However, you can always get a year membership for $120, which includes a Walmart+ membership, free shipping, and other perks.

Sam's Club seems to have more TV deals than Walmart, but Walmart usually has the best deals for budget TVs. Depending on what you're looking for, one might be better than the other.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if you want the most portable way to listen to music on the go, then the best earbuds are a fantastic way to do it. They're tiny, often comfortable, and offer noise cancellation to keep the sounds of the outside world at bay.

At the moment, the AirPods Pro 3 take the crown. But we've spent hundreds of hours testing earbuds to find out which are the best around if you want more than just Apple's offering. They come at a range of different price points to suit any budget, too.

In a recent development, each entry on the list has a quick read section, giving you a brief overview of the buds, followed by longer reviews so that you can get a better idea of how they perform. So let's get straight into it. These are the best wireless earbuds you can buy right now.

We've spent 20 years testing the best earbuds (and the worst; you don't know until they're in your ears) to help you find your next set of portable audio companions.

According to recent reports, the expertise comes from a few places, including our expert reviewers Erin Bashford and Nikita Achanta, who lead our audio testing. Then there's me, Tammy Rodgers, and I've been testing audio equipment for over half a decade, including a time as Tom's Guide's Audio Editor.

Before any earbuds make their way to this guide, here's how we put them through their paces to make sure we only recommend sets we truly believe in and would use ourselves.

Recent findings suggest that when you're looking for newly introduced earbuds, there's a whole range of terminology brands will use to talk about specs and performance. To make things a bit easier, these are the most common terms that come up, and what they mean for you.

According to recent reports, most earbuds come with Active Noise Cancellation (ANC). It uses audio magic and some very clever algorithms to quiet the outside world and make your commute more manageable.

It has been revealed that the earbuds have mics on the outside to pick up external noise. As this passes into your ear, the earbuds generate an opposing frequency to cancel the sound before you hear it. Sometimes this can change the sound of your music, so we'll report when the ANC is either too weak or too invasive.

The EQ, or equalization, allows you to customize the way the earbuds sound. Usually, this means a series of sliders or dials in the companion smartphone app for adjusting the bass, mids or treble. Some manufacturers give you preset EQ options, which save you from getting lost in sliders or graphs.

These are the different sounds that make up your music. You'll generally see them divided into three simple sections: the lows, the mids, and the highs. The lows are the bass frequencies. Think bass guitars and kick drums. You want them to be impactful and low.

The mids are the main parts of your music, like vocals, guitars, and synths. Because they're so important, you want them to be thick and wide. Finally, the highs are cymbals and other higher sounds. These should be crisp and clear.

Tammy is one of Tom's Guide's Buying Guide Editors. She also spends a great deal of her time testing the best earbuds, evaluating them for sound, ANC, comfort and battery life. She's always got at least three pairs of earbuds to choose from at her desk.

Erin is a proud music nerd and needs the best earbuds around. Whether it's eardrum-shedding nu-metal or tranquil folk, she'll listen to it. If a pair of earbuds has awesome sound quality, bouncy ANC and are comfortable? It's an immediate recommendation, regardless of price or brand.

As a music nerd, Nikita is always listening to music. As a reviews writer, she tests earbuds by pushing battery life to the limit and analyzing performance across various genres to answer the question: Are they good value for money? She listens to music almost throughout the day and plays guitar and bass, so she knows how to determine whether a pair of buds reproduces sound well.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The AirPods Pro 3 are the latest version of Apple's popular flagship earbuds. The stem-like design remains, but you get better battery life, an improved fit and more detailed sound. This makes them a worthy upgrade from the AirPods Pro 2, and the gold standard for wireless earbuds. Plus, the Pro 3 have a built-in heart rate monitor and Live Translation (if you have a compatible iPhone).

Recent findings suggest that the AirPods Pro 2 were excellent, but soon aged out compared to the competition. Now, the AirPods Pro 3 have arrived to conquer all and lay waste to Sony and Bose. And, despite a couple of minor flaws, they're right now the best wireless earbuds you can buy right now.

According to recent reports, these are the very best earbuds that Apple has ever made. They've got some key updates over the previous model, for one. There's the extended battery life of eight hours, improved sound quality, and superior noise canceling to keep the noise of your commute at bay.

Those upgrades have materialized in a pair of buds that stun in sound and make sure that your office is a whole lot more tolerable when you're getting on with your day. They lose out to the Sony and Bose due to a lack of codec support for Android devices, but there really is nothing better if you're an iPhone user.

The AirPods Pro 3 improve on the old model in the sound department. They've still got Apple's more neutral sound signature built in, but find more detail and extra bass depth than the older pair.

It has been revealed that they've got a very solid soundstage as well. They're on par with the Sony buds, and better than the Bose alternatives — although there are still options out there that sound better.

Spatial Audio for movies with an Apple TV is still a great way to watch your content, and just as easy to connect up. It works well for music as well, especially when you listen to your music on Apple Music.

Recent findings suggest that the buds have been shrunk this time around, and as a result, have a very comfortable fit. The silicone eartips have been infused with foam for a softer and more comfortable finish, and they mold better to the inner part of your ear.

Recent findings suggest that that means you can wear them for extended periods of time. The sweat and water resistance means you won't have to worry about wearing them when you go to work out, either, hitting an IP57 rating this time around.

The AirPods Pro have always had 'good enough' ANC; powerful but not exceptional. But that changed with the Pro 3, which now almost compete with the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2, but don't quite beat out Bose's buds.

Recent findings suggest that still, it's very good and blocks out all the major noises of your commute or your busy office. It's on par with the Sony WF-1000XM6 — both are excellent noise-canceling options.

Transparency mode is very good as well, and boosts the battery life by another couple of hours. Nice.

Sources indicate that there isn't an app for the AirPods Pro 3, but you can easily adjust their settings from the iPhone settings menu. There, you'll find all their features along with options to update the firmware and change the sound.

Sources indicate that although you can pair the AirPods Pro 3 to an Android phone, I wouldn't really recommend it. You get the bare minimum on a non-Apple phone; a wireless connection. You can't adjust settings, so I'd only suggest the AirPods with an Android phone if you're in a bind.

According to recent reports, much like on the Apple Watch, the battery life for the AirPods has remained stuck for years, allowing the competition to lead ahead. The AirPods 3 Pro buck the trend and, for once, increase the per-bud battery life up to eight hours of ANC listening.

That's a two-hour increase and puts them almost in line with the Sony and Bose sets. If you switch over to the transparency mode, you get 10 hours of battery life, more than pretty much anything else at their price point. That also means you can use the latest Live Translation feature for longer.

The Sony WF-1000XM6 earbuds boast excellent sound quality, customizable EQ, and great battery life. Noise cancellation excels, and the design is also great. These are a highly recommended upgrade for superior quiet and sound control.

Industry observers note that when following up on a highly successful pair of earbuds, there are a couple of things you do. First, you make things better — more features, better sound quality. Then you improve the design — make the fit better, improve the looks.

That’s the WF-1000XM6, Sony’s follow-up to the WF-1000XM5. The AirPods of this generation make a better case for your money if you wield an iPhone, but the XM6 are great for just about everyone else. Just like their predecessor, they’re a fantastic all-rounder, with great specs, sound and ANC.

Recent findings suggest that our four-star review highlights that they’re not entirely perfect. The new case design is a bit odd and makes fitting them into a pocket a chore, and they’re more expensive than the previous model, but those are our only major criticisms.

The sound quality is, as you might expect for something from the WF-1000X series, very good, with support for LDAC. Sony’s excellent DSEE Extreme audio upscaler is here as well, and works a treat. The ANC boasts a massive improvement, too, although Bose still has Sony beat for out-and-out noise performance.

They’re a wonderful pair of comfortable buds with plenty of battery life — there’s little more you could ask for, apart from a discount.

In a recent development, they may seem on the expensive side, but the upgrades in sound performance make them totally worth it. Sony is known for a warmer sound profile on their headphones, and these are a total joy to listen to.

They are only made better by using the personalized EQ settings on the earbuds, and there’s seriously no genre that these buds can’t cope with.

Your favorite songs will sound a lot more detailed, and it’s really awesome to get a studio sound from earbuds instead of having to rely on studio headphones to do the job.

These earbuds are superbly comfortable, and you get a bunch of different eartip options in the box to get the best seal and best security. You can do a fit test to make sure everything fits.

I can wear these buds for hours at a time — they’re seriously comfortable, and they’re lightweight so they never weigh me down.

ANC differs depending on personal experience with these buds. My own experience was amazing, and I couldn’t fault them at all. They made a long travel day on a plane, train, and bus completely silent.

However, another one of my colleagues who tried them out was still able to hear the sounds of traffic moving around. I think it’s all about the eartip fit, so this is an extremely important process to complete.

If you buy this set, just make sure you use the Optimal Earbud Tips feature in the Sound Connect App to get the best fit, and ensure your ANC is working properly.

According to recent reports, the Sound Connect app is one of the most user-friendly I’ve tried. Once you get the hang of things and organize the app to suit the settings you need to use the most, it’s incredibly handy and makes using the earbuds so much better.

The app is where you do all the earbud fit tests and personalized EQ tests to make the overall experience with the buds so much better.

Recent findings suggest that you get eight hours of battery per bud with ANC and 24 hours with the charging case. This is pretty standard and matches up with Apple’s AirPods Pro 3 and the Sony WF-1000XM5.

Industry observers note that the A100 SE are all about sound — pure and simple. There's no feature bloat, no extra AI things, just a pair of great-sounding earbuds with epic battery life. The ANC has fallen behind the competition a little this time around, but they're a great pick for a fantastic price.

Recent findings suggest that the first Cambridge A100 are some of my favorite wireless earbuds — and the SE version are no different. They come in at a price that doesn’t break the bank and offer some of the best sound quality around. For sub-$150, they sound better than buds that cost twice as much — there’s a reason we constantly compare them to the AirPods Pro 3 and others in the review.

They’re refined and classy in their sound, as befits a legacy British Hi-Fi brand. The soundstage is expansive and well layered, and vocals shine. Erin loved the dynamism and vibrancy in her review, noting the accuracy and faithfulness of their representation. High praise indeed.

We had no problems with the comfort as well, and wore them extensively during the testing period. The case is compact and well-shaped (perfect for fitting them into a tighter pocket), and the app is useful and well laid out, though simplistic.

There are just a couple of problems. The ANC isn’t quite up there with other options at a similar price, and the Dolby Atmos mode is, like, bad. But beyond those two bugbears, the A100 SE are the perfect successor to some of our favorite earbuds and a top-notch value pick.

Industry observers note that cambridge has fired a warning shot at just about every other audio manufacturer with the A100 SE. The first model sounded good, but these sound even better. We love how dynamic and clear the buds sound, and the seven-band custom EQ means you can really dial them in.

Industry observers note that they sound better even than more expensive earbuds, and take the fight to options that cost $100-$150 more. That’s the focus of the buds: excellent sound, forget the frills.

There’s warmth here, but it doesn’t overshadow the rest of the sound. Everything is still very clear and expansive, with solid instrument separation. We’re massive fans of the sound.

We scored the buds well for comfort, thanks to their smooth shape and range of different eartips. For the most part, we were able to wear them for long periods without them getting uncomfortable. We didn’t want to rip them out after the workday.

But those with small ears might struggle a little more. These aren’t small buds, and for one tester, they pressed on some parts of their ear. They weren’t uncomfortable, but they knew they were there.

The ANC isn’t going to win them any awards. It’s fine and blocks out some noise, but it’s not as all-encompassing as other options available. If you’re looking for something that blocks out everything, then you might want to think about Sony’s similarly priced options.

Still, if ANC isn’t a priority but you still want some noise blocking, then you won’t find anything to complain about — and the noise-canceling compromise is worth making for that excellent sound.

In a recent development, cambridge’s app is fine, but we did have some problems with some of the features. It became a little buggy at times, with some features not working as they should. A quick restart fixed the issue, but it’s still worth mentioning.

In a recent development, what we really liked, however, was the complete omission of extra feature bloat. There’s everything you might need — an EQ, ANC controls, and that surround mode — but there’s nothing extra. No AI feature, no voice control thing, just what you actually need when using the buds. That’s refreshing.

Battery life is a particular strength of Cambridge's headphones and earbuds. Here, we’ve got 39 hours on tap, 10 hours of bud life. That’s more than just about anything else out there, including buds that cost a whole lot more. It even takes some over-ear headphones to task, and they generally have buds beat for staying power.

It has been revealed that everything charges up quickly, and we found that the battery figures matched up to expectations when we did all of our testing. If you want something that lasts a long time, the A100 SE are a great option.

The Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are the fitness lover's dream. A very comfortable, secure fit so that they stay in place no matter how you move around, and great sound quality to power your workouts. The built-in heart rate monitor is a great cherry on top.

Recent findings suggest that now, I'll be the first to admit that I'm not a fitness expert — but I sure am an earbuds expert. As earbuds, the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are great; there's a reason we ranked them as the best workout headphones you can get right now. They've got excellent ANC from the AirPods Pro 2, and there's some great sound for a solid audio experience.

Industry observers note that given that I'm not a fitness expert, I also spoke to someone who is, so that we can get a picture of why they're on the list. From my review, our fitness expert Nick said:"I genuinely believe that the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are outstanding sports headphones and would be top of my list for people who need an earhook to keep their buds in place during runs and other workouts.".

It's thanks to those secure-fit hooks that keep the earbuds in place no matter how much you run or move around. The heart rate monitor is a nice extra, but we were slightly disappointed with its accuracy.

For all kinds of exercise, the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are an excellent earbud option for everyone.

While not high-fidelity, there's a rhythmic energy to the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 that's infectious. They've got some great bass presence, as you might expect, but they're also good in the upper register too.

They fall down slightly in the mid-range, with a dip in the upper mid-range. That can take the edge off guitars and other instruments, although R&B listeners aren't going to notice too much.

Sources indicate that there's head-tracked Apple Spatial Audio as well for Apple Music listeners, and it works well. It does a number on your battery though, so bear that in mind.

Industry observers note that thanks to their excellent earhook, the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 aren't going anywhere when you do your exercise. It can be a challenge to get them in place, but they're very stable once in.

The buds themselves are comfortable for long periods of wear as well, thanks to the silicone eartip options that you get in the box. The fit finder in the app is good as well, so that you can dial them in perfectly.

The ANC on board is very similar to that which you'll find in the AirPods Pro 2. That means that they're not quite up to speed with the likes of the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2 or the Sony WF-1000XM6, but they still manage to block plenty of noise.

According to recent reports, the transparency modes work well enough, although I found that voices occasionally became fuzzy or tricky to hear depending on the surrounding noise. A shame, but not a deal breaker.

On Apple devices, the Beats are integrated into your settings menu. It works well, with all the options at your fingertips. Android owners have to use the Beats app, which is fine, although we did find some heart rate monitor weirdness on Android devices.

Both methods let you control the ANC and dial in the EQ settings. They're simple, but they work well enough. Android users might find the occasional crash, however.

According to recent reports, the battery life of the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 is exemplary. They feature 10 hours of battery life in the buds themselves, beating out many other options on this list.

That's perfect for long-distance runners and cyclists, or gym-goers who want something that will take them to the gym, last through their exercise, and then take them home again. We found those battery life claims were true in our review. Pop them in the charging case for 45 hours of staying power.

In a recent development, improving on almost every metric compared to the original model (except battery), the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2 are an in-ear noise-canceling triumph. Boosts to ANC and sound quality make them an even better buy than the first model, and the price hasn't increased to match the improved performance.

According to recent reports, the QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds were my favorite release of 2024, and the Gen 2 are now my favorite of 2026. They've improved on pretty much everything over the first model, with the only exception being the unchanged battery life — but it's that world-silencing ANC that really takes them over the edge.

They remain the very best way to listen to music without disruption when you're traveling. That busy train carriage? Silenced. The office? Quietened completely. With that signature orchestral swell, you're in your own world, free to listen to your tunes.

Sound is much better this time around, although you'll still want to adjust the EQ in the Bose app. And you'll be listening comfortably for their entire 6-hour battery life thanks to their incredibly comfortable fit.

I gave them 4.5 stars when I reviewed them, thanks to that all-conquering ANC and solid sound quality. They lose out in the battery department to the XM6, opting instead for out-and-out ANC performance — and there's nothing better to block noise.

The bassy sound of prior Bose earbuds is still here, but it's been refined slightly this time around. There's more detail retrieval, and the soundstage has been extended, but the bass weighting is still very much present.

In a recent development, I've found that dipping into the Bose apps' EQ is a must with any of the brand's headphones. From there, I adjust the bass down slightly and the highs up a few notches to increase the detail and reduce any muddiness. They sound great out of the box, but these improvements make them sound even better.

There's also Immersive Audio, Bose's spatial audio setting. Some like its ability to make music sound much larger, but I find it thins out important frequencies. It also tanks the battery by two hours, making them last an even shorter time.

Yeah, they're still some of the most comfortable buds you can buy. I've been able to wear them for hours and hours at a time without the need to adjust the fit or take them out for a break — they're a lovely thing to have in your ears.

Recent findings suggest that it's all down to the fitting options. There are loads of different silicone tips, and the fit is further improved by the rubber fins you can attach to the edge. They're secure as well, so they won't fall out should you get headbanging or dancing.

Industry observers note that the ANC is the best around — there's nothing that comes close. That's high praise given how good the previous model was at keeping out unwanted sounds, but Bose has somehow made it even better. It's a bit like magic.

You can choose different levels for the noise canceling, but I prefer to leave it on the top level. That way, I don't have to worry about any noise making its way through at all, and I can enjoy my music to the max.

Industry observers note that bose's app is one of the better options around. It's very well laid out, and everything is clearly labeled so that you don't get confused. It even reveals you what's playing, although I'm not entirely sure how useful that feature is.

Sources indicate that it's where you'll find all of the EQ options, noise control, and different sound modes. I particularly like how the app knows what color your buds are — and even lets you name them.

In a recent development, battery life remains a weak point in the QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2's armor. We've still only got six hours' worth of life here, which pales in comparison to some of the competition.

The WF-1000XM6 last for eight hours, a whole two hours more than the QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2. You can't even turn the ANC off to boost the battery life — six hours is all you're going to get.

Recent findings suggest that the Noble Fokus Amadeus are all about one thing and one thing only — their sound quality. Sound quality that blows just about everything else you can buy out of the water. Their ANC is very good, and they're very comfortable, but you buy these for their sound quality.

It has been revealed that the Noble Fokus Amadeus are not cheap. They're more than the AirPods Pro 3, and $50 more than the XM6 and the QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds. They're not the most expensive earbuds around, but you should be ready to shell out if you want a pair.

And you will want a pair, because they've dethroned other excellent-sounding earbuds with their incredibly well-rounded sound signature that dishes out masterful amounts of detail while providing plenty of low-end punch.

According to recent reports, for the price, this is about as close to wired earbuds as you're going to get. The crisp detail is utterly sublime, their mids are fat and juicy, and the bass is tight, controlled, and impactful. An audiophile's wireless dream, one might say, and the latest earbud sound quality standard that all else must be measured against.

In a recent development, the price means they're out of reach for many owners, but as I discovered in my testing, they're well worth their higher price thanks to a very good all-round package. The battery is good, and the ANC matches up — there's very little to get sad about here.

The absolute best thing about the Noble Fokus Amadeus is their sound profile. Thanks to the Audiodo profile in the app it means they sound amazing for everyone too, catering the sound for specific hearing needs.

There are details in my tracks I'd not heard for a while thanks to the impressive detail, and the mids bring plenty of body to listening. The bass kicks and barks with impressive control, notably adding more for drum and bass in particular.

The sound is effortlessly spaced apart for a wide soundstage, and the instruments are very well separated. They sound better than absolutely everything on this list — they're hard to get hold of, but it's worth every single effort when you do.

The Amadeus come with a range of different fitting options in the box for a very comfortable fit. They're more shaped and molded than other options as well, making them easier to wear for longer periods of time.

My favorite fitting options are the flanged tips because they not only improve the sound and the ANC, but they stay in place better than the other options.

While not quite as good as the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2, the ANC is still very good, especially if you opt to use the included flanged tips. It blocks out plenty of noise, focusing on low-end sounds like bus engines.

Sources indicate that transparency mode is nice and natural as well, and makes it easier to talk to shop clerks and bus drivers without needing to take buds out of your ears. There's perhaps a little more noise than some might like, but it's otherwise very good.

It has been revealed that the Noble Fokus app is very simple and lacks some of the more in-depth modes and settings of some of the competition. It's very easy to use, though, and offers everything you actually need.

There's the Audiodo sound customization, as well as a very in-depth EQ to really dial the sound in to your preferred listening curve. You can also change the noise-canceling mode and adjust the volume. Beyond that, there's not much else. At least there's a nice picture of your buds.

According to recent reports, battery life is very solid in the Fokus Amadeus. The buds last for eight hours with the ANC turned on, and 12 hours if you turn the ANC off. They charge swiftly in the case, which provides a total of 42 hours of charge. That's amongst the very best battery life on the list.

Wireless charging is the cherry on top, and a 10-minute quick charge for two hours of use is a nice bonus too.

CMF's latest pair of budget buds are sub-$50 heroes. They pack in loads of premium features, like great customization and even a form of spatial audio. They sound great, fit well, and come in a range of different colors. What's not to like?

Sources indicate that this is a spot that’s likely to be occupied by CMF for some time — the brand's budget buds are just that much better than everyone else's. For just $50 (and often less thanks to significant price drops during deal events), you get earbuds that feel like they’re worth a whole lot more.

CMF has packed in a whole range of great features. There’s sound customization from Dirac, which generally deals with premium Hi-Fi equipment. You get a form of spatial audio to make your music sound bigger, and there’s even great ANC to keep the outside world at bay.

The sound is the most impressive thing here, though. They sound like a pair of buds that cost loads more, and once you’ve gone through the Dirac sound tuning, there’s very little better for under $100. Premium buds — low price.

In a recent development, thanks to CMF’s use of Dirac, the CMF Buds 2 sound excellent. While the core sound is very good, with plenty of bass for impact and revealing detail for interest, the EQ settings kick things up a notch. We’ve described it as “breathing latest life into your songs” — and you’d be hard-pressed to find something at this price that sounds better.

They’re great for a wide range of genres as a result. We spun up everything from the heaviest of metal to breezy folk and classical, and the buds didn’t skip a beat. They’re as meaty as they are delicate — extremely impressive considering the price.

Sources indicate that there’s nothing else that sounds like this at the low price point at which they sit. Even without Dirac, they’re impressive — although you’ll want to run the tuning engine to get the most out of them possible.

Thanks to a multitude of fitting options in the box and a great bud design, the CMF Buds 2 are very comfortable. There are three different sizes, and we found that the ‘small’ size option was perfect for even very small ears.

It has been revealed that there are comfier buds out there, but we had little problem wearing them all day during our testing. More expensive buds might feel slightly nicer in the ear, but these still feel great for the price.

Industry observers note that you can’t expect Bose-level ANC for $50, but you’ll be immediately impressed by the noise-canceling packed into the CMF Buds 2. It does a very good job of keeping the outside world at bay, with some very impressive noise blocking.

Sources indicate that the transparency mode is good too, making it easy to hear what's going on without a robotic edge. They cut down slightly with the ANC during calls — while your voice will be clear, your call partner will be able to hear everything going on around you.

Sources indicate that the Nothing X app is excellent. It's super simple to navigate, with easy access to all the features in the buds. There’s a home screen, and then various menus that are clearly labelled. It’s a must-install if you pick up the CMF Buds 2.

This is where you find the Dirac tuning menu, as well as other settings. Those include the ANC settings, fit test, spatial audio, and touch control settings.

According to recent reports, 11 hours of use in the buds is very solid indeed, and our testing demonstrated no reason to dispute CMF's claims. The case contains 55 hours of use, so you can charge the buds about four times from empty. This is good battery life for buds, better than even some of the more premium options.

Recent findings suggest that samsung's latest buds bring a less AirPods-like case design and excellent sound quality to the table. Some settings and options are locked off for everyone but Galaxy device customers, but they're a great option for the Samsung faithful.

Not one to miss out on a good earbud battle, Samsung’s Galaxy Buds 4 Pro bring a whole host of features to the Samsung crowd who want something that seamlessly integrates with their phone.

According to recent reports, they sound great, and Samsung’s audio upscaling tech is almost as good as Sony’s for improving weaker streams from the likes of Spotify and YouTube Music. That looks like the place Samsung has put the most work into the Galaxy Buds 4 Pro, improving massively over the older model.

It has been revealed that not quite as much work seems to have gone into the battery life, unfortunately. There are only around seven hours on tap with ANC turned on, which lags behind the key competition like the eight hours of the AirPods Pro 3. Still, you get more charge in the case at 30 hours.

Samsung has also packed in some very solid ANC, with loads of clever modes if you wield a Galaxy handset. That’s where their true value lies. There are a bunch of features that only Samsung users will appreciate, like AI translation that only works with Galaxy phones.

If you’re a Galaxy phone user, then the Galaxy Buds 4 Pro were likely already on your shortlist. Thanks to our testing, we can tell you that they’re a great pair of buds that’ll pair with your device perfectly.

“Overall, the Galaxy Buds 4 Pro sound utterly divine” is how Erin finished off the sound portion of the buds review. That’s thanks to rich bass, excellent mids, and great vocals, giving you a top-notch audio experience.

Detail heads might prefer the slightly tighter AirPods or Sony WF-1000XM6, but these sound better than the likes of the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2. Their AI sound enhancement works great with lower-quality streams as well.

In a recent development, thanks to some solid shaping, the Buds 4 Pro are comfortable to wear for long periods of time. There are plenty of fitting options in the box as well to make sure that you’ll find the best fit for you, no matter what shape your ear canals are.

Some with smaller ears might find their slightly larger bodies tighter, but it’s not enough to make them in any way uncomfortable.

The noise canceling is excellent, blocking out all the noise that we could throw at them. They perform about the same as the AirPods and Sony competition, making for more relaxing journeys while wearing them.

According to recent reports, transparency mode is also good, and doesn’t make any of the incoming noise sound robotic. The ANC performance might not be quite as impressive as the Bose buds, but it’s more than a match for the Sony and Apple alternatives.

Some of the headline features, like the AI settings and call enhancement, are only available for Galaxy S23 models and newer. The buds use the Samsung settings menu itself rather than a dedicated app on these devices, and it works well.

There is a Samsung app for other devices, and it's fine. You can control the ANC and other settings, and upgrade the firmware. Still, there are better app experiences for non-Galaxy users, like the Sony and Bose apps.

Battery life is fine. It’s not as good as the eight hours you get from the AirPods or the Sony WF buds, but the seven hours on tap is more than enough to get you through the day. The 30 hours in the charging case, though, make up for the slightly lacking battery life of the buds.

Not every pair of earbuds we test can land on the best list — otherwise, this would just be a list of earbuds that are available to buy. But some are still pretty good and worth considering if you need more options.

Thanks to some key upgrades (mostly in the sound department), the AirPods 5 are a great pair of earbuds, especially with the newly introduced lower price compared to the AirPods 4. The battery life just isn't good enough, however, and compatibility with Android remains an issue that holds them back from a full-chested recommendation.

The EarFun Air Pro 4 bring some excellent features at a bargain price. For a lot less than $100, you get solid ANC, great sound, and a very comfortable fit. They last for ages thanks to their 7.5-hour per-bud battery life, and support loads of hi-res codecs so that your music always sounds its very best.

Read our full EarFun Air Pro 4 review.

The Cambridge Audio Melomania M100 are wonderful earbuds with impeccable sound and a monstrous 52-hour battery life. But the ANC isn't as effective as we'd like, and the case is large and cumbersome to carry around.

Read our full Cambridge Audio Melomania M100 review.

Sony's WF-C710N are well-priced buds that bring some great specs to the table and don't cost the earth. Their ANC is solid, and the sound is very good. We found them comfortable to wear for long periods of time. Whether you like the transparent blue design will probably help you decide if these are right for you.

Read our full Sony WF-C710N review.

The Liberty 5 Pro Max are Soundcore's first entry into the premium earbud space. It is largely successful, with good sound and solid ANC. But at this price, the AirPods Pro 3 or Sony WF-1000XM6 are better value for immersive audio with ANC.

Read our full Soundcore Anker Liberty 5 Pro Max review.

Recent findings suggest that before we make a recommendation about any pair of wireless earbuds, we want to make sure that we've put them through their paces. It helps us find out how good they'll be when you find them in your hands, and makes sure that we can pen our informative, buying advice-packed reviews.

It's all work — no fun. Listening to our favorite music for hours on end to test the sound, taking the earbuds out and about on day trips to test their long-term comfort and ANC algorithm. In all seriousness, we put a lot of effort into making sure that you'll be happy with a purchase you make after reading our buying guides and reviews.

Here are the key factors in our testing and how we evaluate each pair of earbuds that falls across our desks.

Sources indicate that earbuds are going to be jammed directly into your ear holes, so one of the most important things that we test is how comfortable they are over long periods of time, and how difficult it is to dial in the fit. How many bud bits do you get in the box, and are they easy to fit on the buds? Are they loose? Are there extra fitting options like earhooks?

Sources indicate that to find out, we put the buds through their paces. We try out a range of the tips that come with the budsto find the perfect fit that makes the ANC excellent and sound good. After all, if they don't seal well inside of your ear, you're not going to get the best out of your buds. We report our findings, like how easy it was to get the perfect fit, and how comfy they are when dialed in.

In a recent development, then we test their long-term comfort. That means wearing them for hours during a work day, so that we can see how they feel when they're worn for hours on end. If they start impacting certain pressure points in the ear, we'll notice, and it'll go into our review. We're looking for earbuds that can't be felt during wear, so that you forget you're wearing them.

This is my favorite thing to test. Hours and hours of my favorite tunes played into my ears while I work, and I don't have to make excuses to my boss about why I need to be doing it. Excellent news. When we test the audio quality of a pair of buds, we play the Tom's Guide testing playlist on Qobuz so that we can get a good picture of how they sound with some top-quality hi-res tracks to put them through their paces.

We listen at first in a quieter environment so that we can get an idea of how they sound in a vacuum without the ANC to cause potential problems. We compare the earbuds to the sound profiles of those in the best list above, and then we write down our findings for the full review.

It has been revealed that then, we take the earbuds out with the ANC to see if it changes the sound. It might all sound like we're having fun, but there is a point to it all. It gives us a clear picture of the buds' performance in an everyday use case, so that we can see how they'll serve you if you decide you'd like to buy a pair.

Pretty much every pair of earbuds that you can buy today comes with some form of ANC (unless you buy some of the very cheapest ones at the very end of a lengthy Amazon search, you madman), and we want to make sure that it performs well in a variety of use cases.

How do we do it? By taking the earbuds with us wherever we go. That could mean on all our daily commutes, to see if they perform well on the train, or out for hikes so we can see how well they handle normal atmospheric noise. Maybe we're going on a flight — then we can test how well they handle loud engines and crying children.

Once we've thoroughly tested how much noise they block, we also test the transparency modes when we go to buy our tickets or a bag of candies from the grocery store. We look out for how clear the voice of our conversation partner is, and whether they're audible through any other noise. We're also looking out for the quality of the audio that's being pumped in. Is it too loud? Again, we note down our findings for the review.

Recent findings suggest that finally, we want to make sure that the ANC doesn't change the sound of the music too much. After all, you want your music to sound great, and if the ANC changes things too much, it can create annoying sonic challenges.

Given that your earbuds are often going to pull double duty as a form of hands-free calling system, we want to ensure that they're going to be good at it. We make a whole bunch of calls to check things out.

We're looking out for a couple of different things. First of all, we want to make sure that we can hear our call partner well, and that they're coming through clearly. We listen out for clarity and judge whether we can hear them properly throughout the duration of the call, and whether their voice sounds natural.

Industry observers note that then we ask our call partners how we sound. Can they hear us properly, or do the noises of our environment make it hard to hear what we're saying? We note down our findings, and then we report back on them in our review to give you an idea of how they'll perform if you want to take (or make) a call.

We know that manufacturers sometimes have a habit of overestimating their battery life figures. To make sure that you're getting the best information possible, we spend the time testing the battery life claims and whether they ring true. We listen to the buds for hours on end, and count how many hours we used them before they needed to go back into their case. We do this with ANC turned on and with the volume at a comfortable level.

Sources indicate that for charging cases and very long-lasting buds, we extrapolate battery data in a different way. We measure how long we've used them, and then compare that with how much life we've got left. This gives us a good picture of how the battery is going to last in the long run, and whether you'll get those rated claims.

Industry observers note that hopefully, we've managed to curate a list of wireless earbuds that hit the mark for you. But if you're still not sure how to choose between them, these are some additional pointers.

What do you want out of your buds?

Sources indicate that there are as many reasons to buy earbuds as there are earbuds themselves. You need to work out what you're looking for first and foremost — it's why I've divided the list up into the most important headline features.

Recent findings suggest that do you want the best sound, and would you be willing to give up some battery life and pay a bit more for it? If not, then you should go for the best earbuds overall, but if you don't mind some compromise, then you should go for the best-sounding earbuds.

It has been revealed that it's key to make a list of the features that are most important to you, and then work out from there which of the earbuds on the list fit those criteria the best. After all, what might be the best for one person might not be the best for you.

Do you want headphones or earbuds?

If you're looking for the most compact, easily transported audio device around, then the best earbuds are probably going to be right for you. But there are a couple of things to remember: they're going to live inside your ears, and not everyone likes the feeling of in-ears after longer periods of listening.

Industry observers note that if you'd prefer something more comfortable for longer periods of wear that offers more battery life, and potentially better audio quality, you should consider some of the best wireless headphones. They might cost a bit more, but you might be more comfortable.

Repairability is becoming ever more important, as we try to find newly introduced ways to lengthen the life of our devices, but also look after the planet that we call home. Repairing products is great for both, and it's important to consider it when buying new tech.

Unfortunately, earbuds are one of those products that are extremely rarely user-repairable. Thanks to their size and the amount of tech that companies have to pack into their buds, it's generally impossible to make the insides accessible to you or me.

According to recent reports, not all is lost, however — some manufacturers do offer some form of repair service, so you don't have to worry if your buds stop working. But this is still pretty rare, so if this is a priority for you, it's worth picking up a pair of the Fairphone Fairbuds 2.

There are seven user-repairable components; they cost less than $100 and come in two colors. Tom's Guide Managing Editor James Frew rated the first generation, but they weren't available in the U.S. That all changed with the Fairbuds 2, which you can buy directly from Fairphone.

I talk about this on our best headphones list, but I think it's worth reiterating here. It's easy to get hooked on frequency response graphs and numbers, and think you're getting a surefire cheat code to finding the best-sounding earbuds.

You'll spot them as a pair of numbers in spec lists, like "15 Hz-22 kHz." The first number is how low the earbuds can go, and the second is how high they can go.

You might think that finding a pair with the greatest frequency range is going to net you a pair of excellent-sounding earbuds. While that can be true, it's not worth seeking out. Just because a pair of earbuds can go really low doesn't mean they're good at replicating those frequencies, and neither does it tell you about what's going on in the music itself.

There's only one way to really tell how good a pair of earbuds is — and that's to give them a listen. Or, of course, you could read one of our excellent and informative earbuds reviews.

With the release of the prequel The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, franchise producer Nina Jacobson regrets splitting the Mockingjay films into two parts.

At the time, The Twilight Saga and Harry Potter split their grand finale into two films, and Lionsgate followed suit, breaking up the last Suzanne Collins book of the OG Hunger Games trilogy into two films as well.

“Even though I love the Mockingjay films, if I had it to do over again, I think both Francis [Lawrence, director] and I might try to do it all in one,” she mentioned in an interview with Empire.

She continued, “Mockingjay was such a substantial book, and it takes you to so many different places. But in the end, I think that Francis and I both felt that splitting them up… even if it did come from an inside-out place of really feeling like we needed two films to tell the story, I think audiences find it cynical. Even if its intentions are earnest, which they were. They feel like it’s a play to make them see two films instead of one.” Watch on Deadline.

With Collins’ two prequels like The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes and Sunrise on the Reaping, producers have changed the way they adapt the books.

Recent findings suggest that “We really put the burden on ourselves [now], even when it’s a major book, to transform it into a theatrical experience, to not take advantage of your audience’s patience, to make it as tight as we can,” Jacobson told the publication. “[Sunrise On The Reaping] is the longest by a minute or two of all of them.”.

Sources indicate that the Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping sees Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson, and Woody Harrelson return to their roles from the original trilogy. The film stars Joseph Zada playing a young Haymitch, and is joined by Mckenna Grace, Whitney Peak, Glenn Close (Drusilla), Ralph Finneas (President Snow), Billy Porter (Magno), Maya Hawke (Wiress), Elle Fanning (Effie), Percy Daggs IV (Ampert), Whitney Peak (Lenore Dove), Lili Taylor (Mags), Kiran Culkin (Caesar Flickerman), Kelvin Harrison Jr (Beetee), Jesse Plemons (Plutarch), Ben Wang (Wyatt), among others.

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (485 w)

Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5mac ↗ Open Full Page

An annoying ‘mistake’ in macOS was actually prep for the latest MacBook Pro

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (485 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You may remember that Apple made a seeming mistake in the user interface for macOS 26, meaning that attempts to resize windows would often fail.
  • According to recent reports, I was one of a number of people to note that trying to grab the corner of a window in macOS Tahoe in order to resize it would often fail.
  • According to recent reports, it turns out that my initial click in the window corner instinctively happens in an area where the window doesn’t respond to it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You may remember that Apple made a seeming mistake in the user interface for macOS 26, meaning that attempts to resize windows would often fail. The reason for this has now become clear, and Apple has done something both fun and clever in macOS 27 to resolve it ….

According to recent reports, I was one of a number of people to note that trying to grab the corner of a window in macOS Tahoe in order to resize it would often fail. Developer Norbert Heger pointed out this is because Apple changed the radius of the corners without changing the grabbable area.

According to recent reports, it turns out that my initial click in the window corner instinctively happens in an area where the window doesn’t respond to it. The window expects this click to happen in an area of 19 × 19 pixels, located near the window corner. If the window had no rounded corners at all, 62% of that area would lie inside the window. But due to the huge corner radius in Tahoe, most of it – about 75% – now lies outside the window.

According to recent reports, at the time, the radius change itself looked like an inexplicable mistake on Apple’s part, and the firm did revert it. However, Macworld’s Michael Simon appears to have discovered the reason for the original change.

The fresh rounder corners on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR are basically a perfect match for the macOS 26 radii.

Recent findings suggest that so if you move a window to the corner of the fresh machine, it would fit perfectly. However, since Apple reverted the corner radius, it would no longer do so. The organization solved this by a clever UI transition.

What’s happening there is Golden Gate’s 20-point corner radius is subtly and gradually expanding when It approaches the bottom corner of the screen to match the exact corner of the display, which is much larger. I can’t be certain it’s exactly 26-point, but it sure looks like it to me. The effect is incredible. I’ve watched it like 20 times and I can barely see it changing, yet when it reaches the corner it’s perfectly expanded to match.

You can see this illustrated by a GIF in the Macworld piece. While the original change annoyed me, Apple’s solution is the perfect example of the company sweating the details.
